stories.headline: EAM Jaishankar warns of ‘major food crisis’ in coming months
stories.deck: "We are today looking at a situation where some of the major grain exporters will not be able to send out their shipments, particularly out to the Black Sea," S. Jaishankar said
stories.bodyText:
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has warned of a “major food crisis” in the coming months, in addition to the already significant fertiliser shortages the world is witnessing due to the Ukraine and Iran conflicts, saying the situation is “very very stressful” for Global South economies.
“… this is a big concern for us, which is, if you look at these two conflicts, the Ukraine and now the Iran-Gulf conflict, they've actually had a devastating impact on Global South economies,” Mr. Jaishankar said during a conversation hosted at Asia Society in New York on Monday (September 28, 2026).
He said there is particular concern about the energy situation as the "market is very tight” and on top of that, if “people play politics with it, that adds to the complications in the market,” as that will drive up prices at a time when people should actually be stabilising prices.
“So part of it is actually the security of oil supplies, and part of it is the politics of oil supplies, and they are feeding into each other, and they are creating a double crisis or an aggravated crisis,” he said.
On the concerning food situation amid the raging global conflicts, Mr. Jaishankar said, "We are today looking at a situation where some of the major grain exporters will not be able to send out their shipments, particularly out to the Black Sea."
He said that the world is looking at significant fertiliser shortages because the key producers are in West Asia and Russia, and their fertiliser production has been impacted.
Combined with impacts of climate patterns like a super El Niño, Mr. Jaishankar said, “there is going to be a major food crisis probably in the coming months. So if you have energy as a big crunch, and then food and fertilisers on top of it, and finance because every time there's a conflict, money moves towards safe harbours and away from the Global South, the net result of it has been really very very stressful.”
He said policymakers can't say that such a situation was not intended.
“Countries should not be so self-centred that they're in their own world and take your decision and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’.”
Mr. Jaishankar said that “sound common sense” should ensure that the basic needs of a whole lot of countries should not be so neglected that they are put in distress situations. “And that is a concern that we have.”
Mr. Jaishankar said the energy crisis is creating instability.
“We have already seen it after the Ukraine war. We saw in our neighbourhood the direct result of that in political instability, and my fear is what is happening in Iran and the Gulf is going to feed, is going to aggravate,” he said.
On countries coming under pressure, he said there would be countries that would obviously maintain their independence and their autonomy.
“Some others would find it harder to do so. So those of us who are autonomous, we'd like to see more of us who are autonomous. But it’s not a black-and-white scenario. It would depend on the issue and the stakes involved. There'll be cases where countries would make adjustments. There'll be cases where they would fight back,” he said.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026 India’s medallists: Full list of winners
stories.deck: Here’s the full list of Indian medallists at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 categorised by sport
stories.bodyText:
The 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games are underway in Japan. India is currently placed at the 10th spot on the medals’ table with 52 medals. China is leading the table with 254 medals. Japan is second with 183 medals and Republic of Korea is third with 96 medals.
On Tuesday (September 29, 2026), the quartet of Kiran Pahal, M.R. Poovamma, Prachi Choudhary and Vithya Ramraj won India’s first and only track-and-field gold medal at the Asian Games in Nagoya.
Indian boxer Narender Berwal won the men’s +90kg bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games after losing to reigning world champion Aibek Oralbay of Kazakhstan in the semi-finals on Tuesday (September 30, 2026).
Gulveer Singh added a third medal to his tally at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, clinching bronze in the men’s 5000m on Tuesday.
India’s mixed 4x100m relay quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha S.S., Animesh Kujur and Harita Bhadra clinched bronze at the Asian Games.
India’s Pooja Singh secured the bronze medal in the women’s high jump at the 2026 Asian Games on Tuesday after clearing 1.84m in the final.
The quartet of Manu T.S., Dharmveer Choudhary, Jay Kumar and Vishal T.K. clinched bronze in the men’s 4x400m relay final on Tuesday.
Neeru Dhanda scripted history on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), becoming the first Indian shooter to win an Asian Games gold medal in the women’s individual trap event, while also breaking the continental record in the process.
Indian shooters Neeru Dhanda, Aashima Ahlawat and Manisha Keer clinched silver in the women’s trap team event at the Asian Games.
On September 28, 2026, Vithya Ramraj won a bronze medal in 400 M hurdles in a sensational run that clocked 54.75 seconds and broke her own national record she had jointly held with athlete PT Usha.
Murali Sreeshankar and Gulveer Singh claimed silver medals in the long jump and 1500m, respectively, while Parul Chaudhary secured bronze in the women’s 5000m, adding a second medal to her Aichi-Nagoya campaign.
India also bagged two medals in the javelin throw, with Yash Vir Singh winning silver and Rohit Yadav taking bronze, behind Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga.
Earlier that day, Indian shooter Esha Singh clinched a silver medal in the women’s 25m pistol individual competition.
Pincky Balhara became the first Indian to win two Kurash medals at the Asian Games after clinching bronze on Monday (September 28, 2026), following a 0-5 semifinal defeat to South Korea’s Sumin Mo in the women’s 78kg event.
On Sunday (September 27, 2026), India’s Abhay Singh settled for an Asian Games silver medal after going down against Eain Yow Ng of Malaysia in the men’s singles final of the squash competition, and junior world champion Anahat Singh similarly secured a hard-fought Silver in the women’s singles final against Malaysia’s Sivasangari Subramaniam.
Harita Bhadra clinched bronze in the women’s 200m at the Asian Games. Long jumper Ancy Sojan secured silver in the women’s long jump, while Sarvesh Kushare claimed silver in the men’s high jump.
Tejaswin Shankar, meanwhile, secured his second Asian Games medal, winning bronze in the decathlon following the two-day competition.
Parul Chaudhary bettered her personal best on her way to bronze in the women’s 3000m steeplechase at the Asian Games.
On Saturday (September 26), India’s Sawan Barwal won a silver medal in the men’s marathon. India’s women’s kabaddi team extended their dominance at the Asian Games securing yet another gold medal after a thrilling 37-34 win over Iran in the finals. The men’s hockey team continued it’s winning streak, defeating Japan by 2-0, securing the semifinal berth in the big-ticket sports event.
Simultaneously, the squash squad led by teen-sensation Anahat Singh and Abhay Shetty in singles category stormed into the final game. The duo will be competing for a gold medal in their final game on Sunday.
Women’s 50m rifle 3P team comprising of Vidarsa Vinod, Ashi Chouksey, Tilottama Sen won the silver medal. Mixed squash doubles team including Joshana Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar clinched the bronze medal.
On Friday (September 25), the duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze medal in table tennis mixed doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Baranica Elangovan entered her name in the record books by winning a historic bronze medal for India in the women’s pole vault event at the Asian Games
Indian long-distance runner Gulveer Singh upgraded his Asian Games medal from bronze to silver in the men’s 10,000m.
India’s Manpreet Kaur clinched the bronze medal in women’s shot put competition of the Asian Games with an effort of 17.17m in Nagoya on Friday (September 25).
Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh won gold in the mixed team 10m air pistol event. The Indian team, comprising Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar, Rudranksh Patil and Niraj Kumar, won silver in the men’s 50m rifle 3P team event.
The Indian 4x400m mixed relay quartet of Vishal T.K., M.R. Poovamma, Manu T.S. and Vithya Ramraj earned a silver medal in the final at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium.
Manpreet Kaur clinched a bronze medal in the Women’s Shot Put final with a season-best throw of 17.17 meters.
The duo of Manush Shah and Diya Chitale secured a historic bronze in Table Tennis Mixed Doubles after stunning the world No. 4 pair from Hong Kong to enter the semi-finals.
Seema Kumari, competing in her first Asiad, won a bronze medal in the 10,000m at the Asian Games, 16 years after Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut’s historic gold-silver double in 2010.
Manipur’s Naorem Roshibina Devi won her third consecutive Asian Games medal, clinching silver after losing to Zhang Xiaoyu in the women’s 60kg wushu final on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Jay Meena secured India’s first-ever soft tennis medal at the Asian Games, fetching a bronze after losing to Japan’s Takuya Kurosaka in the men’s singles semifinals. Star Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu completed her medal collection, winning a silver medal in the women’s 49kg event in the Asian Games.
Lakshya Sen and Ayush Shetty faltered against higher-ranked opponents as the Indian men’s team concluded with a bronze medal after losing 1-3 to their rivals, China, in the semifinals.
The Indian Women’s Cricket Team clinched a historic victory at the Karogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Aichi. Facing off against Sri Lanka in a high-stakes final, the Women in Blue triumphed to secure India’s very first gold medal of the tournament.
Meanwhile, shooters have led the charge for India. The women’s skeet team, comprising Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal, won a bronze with a combined score of 331 here on September 23, 2026.
Experienced rifle shooter Elavenil Valarivan played a starring role in the country’s double-silver haul in the women’s 10m air rifle competition. Elavenil, one of India’s most accomplished rifle shooters, helped the country secure silver in the team event along with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod. She then went on to add an individual silver.
For the men’s side, teenager Himanshu Dhillon produced a superb performance to win silver, while former world champion Rudrankksh Patil clinched bronze as India secured two individual podium finishes in the men’s 10m air rifle event. The two then teamed up with Parth Mane to win another silver in the team event, finishing just behind China.
After an impressive start in shooting, India also managed to script history in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), with Suchika Tariyal winning the nation’s first-ever bronze medal for MMA at the Asian Games.
A contingent of 501 Indian athletes, comprising 267 men and 234 women, is competing across 36 disciplines in the 2026 edition. Apart from shooting, athletics and archery too are expected to add to the medal tally. India is also defending both the men’s and women’s titles in cricket and kabaddi.

stories.headline: FCRA bill improvement on existing law, says government
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The vesting of assets is the single-most contentious provision in the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill but the law ministry on Tuesday said the proposal was, in fact, an improvement upon the existing law as its structured framework enhanced legal certainty, administrative efficiency and accountability in managing foreign-funded assets.
The current law provides for vesting of assets but does not specify the nature, duration and finality of such vesting, the ministry told a joint committee of Parliament, which is examining the bill, adding that it led to an open-ended custodial arrangement and administrative difficulties in managing assets, sources said.
The ministry was represented by legislative secretary Rajiv Mani at the meeting where State Bank of India, the only bank designated to receive foreign contributions at its New Delhi main branch, supported the bill’s objectives but made a host of suggestions, flagged concerns and sought more clarity, including on how to handle an organisation’s accounts and deposits when its permission to receive foreign donations ends.
MPs from opposition parties and BJP clashed over provisions of the bill with two DMK MPs, A Raja and P Wilson, dubbing the bill violative of Article 300(A), which says no one will be deprived of their property save by the authority of law.
They argued that the Supreme Court has in its rulings explained the ground on which the govt can seize properties and the FCRA bill was violative of this. BJP MP Nishikant Dubey said laws overseeing trusts and societies had similar provisions for seizure of assets.
Turning to alleged misuse of foreign money for conversion, he said this allowed a person converted to a minority religion to enjoy twin quota benefits in some cases, which violated the right to equality. A team of senior SBI officials led by its chairperson C S Setty said while the bill provided for govt control of foreign contributions and assets in such cases, it left the detailed banking procedure to be prescribed in rules, sources said.

SBI officers flagged a potential gap between the date when a registration ceased and the date the bank was informed. There is no express protection for banks acting in good faith on the instructions of the designated authority or the home ministry, they said.
The bank said it supported a clear legal framework for managing foreign contributions when an organisation’s registration ended. It called for detailed rules, common procedures for banks and prompt updates on registration status before the new provisions take effect.

stories.headline: Supreme Court allows forensic audit in Fortis case
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld a Delhi HC order directing forensic audit of dissipation of shares of Fortis Healthcare Ltd (FHL) and Fortis Healthcare Holdings Pvt Ltd (FHHPL) through 17 banks and financial institutions allegedly to frustrate execution of a decade-old Rs 5,300 crore foreign decree by Daiichi Sankyo against brothers Malvinder and Shivinder Singh.
Brushing aside a challenge to the forensic audit order of the HC by senior advocate Shyam Divan, appearing on behalf of Yes Bank and Axis Bank, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana clarified the forensic audit would not be a roving inquiry against the banks or FIIs but will focus on the transaction of shares of FHL and FHHPL.
The bench also chided Daiichi for giving up its plea for forensic audit of the dissipation of shares in the two companies, which was a major window for the banks to argue that HC could not have passed the order for forensic audit when decree holder had given up that plea.
Daiichi counsel Arvind Datar told the court that the foreign decree, upheld by SC, had not been implemented for a decade and the plea giving up forensic audit was made due to frustration over the long lapse of time in executing the decree in India.
Share your thoughts in the comments
Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
In fact, Delhi HC judge Justice Subramonium Prasad started his Aug 31 judgement quoting an 1872 judgement of Fort William HC (Calcutta HC) which stated “the difficulty of a litigant in India begins when he has obtained a decree”.
Delhi HC had said in its judgment, “For the loans taken by the downstream entities of the judgment-debtors (Singh brothers and their companies), shares of FHL held by FHHPL were kept as security. This court needs to ascertain whether these loans were part of a legitimate transaction for the genuine business or were they part of the fraud to dissipate the shareholding of FHHPL in FHL to defeat the decree.”
While directing the forensic auditor to identify each dealing in shareholdings aimed at frustrating the decree, Justice Prasad had asked it to examine “the role of banks, and identify the loan facilities secured by FHL shares, the creation and variation of security, maintenance of security margins, operation of contractual top-up obligations, invocation and sale of pledged shares, release of security, and the outstanding liability corresponding to each transaction”.

briefs.headline: Maharashtra FDA tightens infant food rules, bans formula promotions and influencer advertising
briefs.bodyText:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a statewide compliance order tightening the manufacture, sale, labelling and promotion of infant foods and milk substitutes, citing concerns over breastfeeding practices and emerging health risks among children and adolescents as part of the need for stricter enforcement.
The order, issued by Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe under Section 30 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, brings enforcement of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, alongside the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, under a single enforcement mechanism.
The order, which came into force immediately, applies across the supply chain, including manufacturers, brand owners, importers, re-packers, distributors, retailers, pharmacies, hospital suppliers and e-commerce platforms dealing with infant formula, infant milk food, follow-up formula, complementary and traditional infant foods, foods for special medical purposes and feeding bottles.
Among violations flagged by the FDA during inspections and surveys were labels without mandatory breastfeeding notices, age-of-introduction and preparation warnings, as well as products marketed under descriptions such as "baby cereal", "health mix", "stage food" and "nutrition powder" to evade prescribed standards.
Under the order, packages must prominently display the notice, "IMPORTANT NOTICE – MOTHER'S MILK IS BEST FOR YOUR BABY", on the front. Pictures of infants or women are prohibited, as are descriptions such as "humanised", "maternalised", "complete food" and "health food". Complementary foods must also state that they should be introduced only after six months.
The FDA said the stricter enforcement also comes against the backdrop of health and breastfeeding trends highlighted through National Family Health Survey (NFHS)-6 data. According to data cited while explaining the measure, only 55.8% of mothers initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, falling to 52.8% in urban areas.
Officials also pointed to health indicators among children and adolescents, including data showing 35.1% of those aged 10-19 with high blood pressure and 12.3% classified as prediabetic or diabetic. High triglyceride levels and low HDL cholesterol have also been reported in this age group. The FDA linked these trends to concerns over improper infant and childhood feeding practices and the longer-term burden of non-communicable diseases.
The compliance order imposes a complete prohibition on advertisements, free samples, gifts, coupons, cashback, discount campaigns, influencer promotions and cross-promotions of infant milk substitutes, infant foods and feeding bottles, including on e-commerce marketplaces, social media and messaging applications.
Companies are also barred from providing sponsorship, funding, hospitality, travel or registration expenses, speaker fees, research grants or other benefits to health workers, hospitals, nursing homes, pharmacies or medical associations in connection with conferences, seminars, workshops, continuing medical education programmes, fellowships or research activities.
Responding to questions over promotions in the grey areas of social-media advertising, Mr. Mundhe said responsibility could extend to both the company marketing the product and the person endorsing it if the promotion violates the law.
The FDA has also put in place an online system with time-stamped records of complaints and inspections, which officials said is intended to ensure transparency in enforcement and guard against corruption or extortion during inspections.
Manufacturers, importers and brand owners have been given 30 days to conduct self-audits of their licences, product approvals, BIS coverage, formulations, labels and promotional practices and submit compliance declarations. Designated Officers have 45 days to map establishments and online sellers and begin risk-based inspections, while the first consolidated enforcement report is to be submitted to the Commissioner within 60 days.
Violations can attract penalties of up to ₹10 lakh for misleading advertisements or unlicensed businesses, ₹5 lakh for substandard food and ₹3 lakh for misbranded food. Unsafe food can also lead to prosecution, with imprisonment extending up to life imprisonment where consumption results in death. Licences can additionally be suspended or cancelled.
Mr. Mundhe, however, distinguished prohibited commercial promotion from legitimate medical advice. The restrictions do not prevent medical practitioners from providing necessary nutritional guidance where a mother is unable to breastfeed for medical reasons or where an infant requires food for specialised medical purposes. The prohibition is aimed at commercial promotion of substitutes rather than medically necessary advice, he said.
The FDA said the broader objective of the enforcement drive is to encourage healthy feeding practices and ensure safe nutrition during the early years of life, which officials described as crucial to children's physical and intellectual development.
"A child under two cannot protect itself," Mr. Mundhe said, adding that enforcement of the IMS Act would now be the responsibility of every Food Safety Officer in Maharashtra and would be undertaken as rigorously as enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards Act.

briefs.headline: Oil stays above $103 after Trump denies easing sanctions on Iran
briefs.deck: Rising oil prices are reflecting a renewed uncertainty over US sanctions on Iran, with Brent crude surpassing $103 a barrel and WTI hovering around $89. As Qatar works hard to ease tensions between the United States and Iran, Saudi Arabia has resumed oil exports from the Red Sea, aiding recovery in regional supply.
briefs.bodyText:
Oil prices inched higher on Wednesday, trading beyond the $103 per barrel mark as uncertainty over the US stance towards Iran returned to the spotlight. US The momentum came after US President Donald Trump rejected a report that Washington was prepared to ease sanctions on Tehran. Qatar, meanwhile, said it was continuing efforts to bring Iran and the US towards an agreement.
Brent crude rose 0.56% to $103.20, while WTI crude gained 0.11% to $89.48. The gains came a day after oil prices declined as crude supplies from the Middle East showed signs of recovering.
As the Strait of Hormuz remains choked for a seventh month, oil prices have continued to rise. Brent is set to gain around 14% in September, which would be its biggest monthly increase since July. WTI is headed for a rise of about 4% after crossing $106 for the first time since May.
The gap between Brent and WTI has also widened to its highest level in four months this month. Traders have been assessing possible US restrictions on diesel exports, which could result in an oversupply in the domestic market and reduce the amount of crude processed by US refiners.
Trump is considering allowing sales of red-dyed diesel instead of imposing an export ban, according to Reuters. 
The move would be aimed at offering some relief to consumers as the November mid-term elections approach.
Qatar seeks common ground
Qatar on Tuesday said that it hoped its shuttle diplomacy between Iran and the US could help the two sides reach a breakthrough.
"We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said.
The diplomatic efforts came amid a report by Axios that cited US officials as saying Trump was willing to offer Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in return for "concrete" steps by Tehran on its nuclear programme.
Trump rejected the report, saying "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING."
Middle East supply picks up
The recovery in regional oil flows has also emerged as a key factor for the market. Saudi Arabia resumed oil tanker loadings from its Red Sea port of Yanbu on Tuesday after restarting operations on the East-West Pipeline.
Oil exports from Middle Eastern producers rose to 16.328 million barrels per day in September, their highest level since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February.
US inventory figures also remained in focus. Crude oil and gasoline stocks increased last week, while distillate inventories declined, according to market sources citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.
US crude inventories rose by 1.02 million barrels in the week ended September 25, the sources said.
The official US Energy Information Administration inventory data is due at 10:30 a.m. EDT (1430 GMT). Analysts polled by Reuters expect crude and product inventories to have declined.

briefs.headline: India-China ties have improved in last couple of years: EAM
briefs.bodyText:
NEW YORK: The ties between India and China are “better” today than they were a couple of years ago, external affairs minister 
S Jaishankar
 said, underlining that as border issues are resolved, the relationship returns to normalcy.
He was responding to a question on India-China relations, which have seen an upswing in recent times, including President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to India for the Brics Leaders’ Summit hosted by New Delhi.
“If you asked me, compared to where you were in 2025, is the relationship better today? I would say yes. Compared to 2024, even more so,” Jaishankar said during a conversation hosted at Asia Society on Monday. He said it was not so much a “structural change”, but part of the reason things had improved was that “they had gone so much off-track that the moment you stabilised it, it was going to improve”.

After the 2020 border standoff, the relationship had been impacted, he said.
Following the standoff, all “normal contacts” between the two nations had halted, though “trade was continuing”. Official exchanges, visa issuance and flights were impacted. “So once the border standoff was resolved, it was natural that this would start to improve,” he said.

briefs.headline: U.S. forces exit Iraq after two decades, leaving opening for Iran
briefs.deck: While the eventual departure of U.S. forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday (September 30, 2026), a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.
Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal — agreed in 2024 under then- President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran — could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other U.S. enemies to stage a comeback, including Islamic State.
“Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition’s departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a counterweight to Tehran’s influence in Iraq,” said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specialising in studying armed Shi’ite groups aligned with Iran.
He predicted that the pro-Iranian militia groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also “seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making”. Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the U.S. withdrawal as “a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honorable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project”.
“On September 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country,” he told Reuters. “Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people.”
Not ready
While the eventual departure of U.S. forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature. “We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time,” Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, told Reuters.
“All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the [U.S.-led coalition] leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear.” American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Sunni Muslim dictator Saddam Hussein, and went on to occupy the country, install a Shi’ite-led government and fight a years-long counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011.
They returned less than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group Islamic State in a major war from 2014 to 2017. Around twice as many Americans died in “Operation Iraqi Freedom” as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt U.S. withdrawal in 2021.
In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield.
The United States killed a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran’s allies repeatedly fired on U.S. bases, sometimes drawing reprisals.
In this year’s war against Iran, 7 of the 18 U.S. service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Victory for Iran’s axis
Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire West Asia, casts the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region. “Lasting security will prevail in Iraq” once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran’s Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Monday (September 28, 2026).
Iran “welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it,” he told Iran’s parliamentary news service. “Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops.” Washington has accused Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence.
New life for Islamic State?
Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the U.S. pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network. At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former U.S. military base.
A lack of U.S. intelligence, logistical support and drones will give Islamic State a chance to regroup, said Kurdish commander Sirwan Barzani.
“For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by [Islamic State] sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September,” he said. “This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale” of the fighters.
Iraqi security forces said a suspected Islamic State cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout. The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials.
Islamic State “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” said Colonel Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

briefs.headline: Pakistan airspace closed, India eyes China skies
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India is trying to work out a “Pakistan bypass” with China for its domestic airlines as the latest closure since April 2025 has made routes between Delhi and West unviable due to longer detours amid soaring oil prices. India is in talks with China to make the Hotan route in Xinjiang available to its airlines.
The Hotan plan has been in the works for months, with Air India and IndiGo doing feasibility studies. AI’s Boeing 777s, B787s and Airbus A350s can take the route. IndiGo can do so after it starts getting A350s.
“We are exploring alternate airspaces and Hotan is under discussion. Diplomatic-level talks are underway. We are strongly pushing for Hotan. We are asking Indian airlines to launch more international flights from other parts of India (where western routes are not impacted by Pak airspace closure) like the south and improve connectivity from there,” aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu said on the sidelines of Routes Asia 2027 Tuesday.
India is keen on a Pakistan bypass as international travel is growing at about 5% over the past decade, while airlines’ growth plans are hit by the neighbour’s airspace closures. 
To be sure, India also reciprocally closes its airspace for Pak airlines but their operations are mainly to the West.
Air India, which lost Rs 4,000 crore due to Pakistan airspace closure in a year, had made a presentation on the Hotan waypoint route.
Some AI wide body aircraft have additional oxygen storage, allowing them more time to step descend to 14,000 feet and then 10,000 feet in case of single engine failure or cabin de-pressurisation while flying out of the region.
This is the second time in five years that Air India has found an alternate way around an airspace closure. Before Aug 2021, AI flights used the Pakistan-Afghanistan-Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan route. After Taliban took over Kabul, AI took the longer route via south Pakistan and then Iran-Turkey. In a few months, Air India found a way out by overflying the Hindu Kush.
Share your thoughts in the comments
Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
A plane gets lighter as it burns fuel, allowing it to ascend. A wide body taking off from Delhi for Europe or North America is tanked up for the non-stop journey and must overfly the Hindu Kush, where minimum altitude is 30,000 feet. The tallest mountain is 25,289-foot Terich Mir.
Air India finalised the Hindu Kush route for the B787 after one-and-a-half months of simulator studies as it could fly at about 35,000 feet. For the heavier B777, it took under four months to finalise procedures for overflying Hindukush and ensure it also maintained 30,000 feet.

briefs.headline: Walking a tightrope: 5 hurdles facing Noel Tata and an unlisted Tata Sons
briefs.deck: Noel Tata's plan for merging Tata companies seeks to maintain the private status of Tata Sons, avoiding any public listing. However, the Reserve Bank of India has already rejected previous requests to ease regulatory restrictions on Tata Sons. Additionally, potential dissent within the Tata Sons board may question the validity of this merger initiative, amplified by the Shapoorji Pallonji Group's…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Noel Tata’s plan to keep 
Tata Sons
 private faces five hurdles, the steepest of which is a 
Reserve Bank of India
 (RBI) that has already refused to release the group’s holding company from its rules. The chairman of Tata Trusts has proposed merging Tata Electronics Systems Solutions and Tata Consulting Engineers into Tata Sons, a move designed to take the holding company outside the RBI’s upper-layer NBFC and Core Investment Company regulations, and so avoid a public listing. Success depends on winning over his own trustees, a divided Tata Sons board, the central bank, an aggrieved minority shareholder and a 75% vote he cannot yet count on.
Tata Trusts
Dissent persists at home. Noel emailed the merger proposal to trustees Monday in his capacity as chairman of Tata Trusts, relying on a July 28, 2025 resolution. But some trustees said the resolution empowered N Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, not Noel, to keep Tata Sons unlisted and to engage with the RBI. They added that no board meeting was held to weigh the proposal before it was unveiled. They also questioned whether the Tata Sons board can consider the plan without approval from both the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), the latter currently under a regulatory restriction.
The Tata Sons board
The board is split 5:1, and the majority sees a listing as the simplest route to compliance. Noel can seek a board meeting to consider the plan, but he needs the backing of fellow Trusts nominee director Venu Srinivasan. 
On Noel’s reading of Article 121 of Tata Sons’ Articles of Association, the merger fails if one Trusts nominee votes against. By Tata Sons’ reading, if the Trusts’ nominees vote in different directions, the result would be a split and Chandrasekaran would have the chairman’s casting vote. Srinivasan had backed Chandrasekaran’s reappointment; only Noel had opposed. Add the majority view that an IPO offers greater regulatory certainty than a restructuring, and the outcome looks stacked against Noel.
Reserve Bank’s NOC
The regulator is the most formidable obstacle. Earlier this month it rejected Tata Sons’ application to surrender its CIC registration, even though the company had repaid more than Rs 30,000 crore of debt. That keeps alive the requirement to comply with the upper-layer NBFC-CIC rules including listing. The merger is designed to ensure Tata Sons no longer qualifies as an NBFC or a CIC, but the RBI’s 2025 NBFC-voluntary amalgamations directions require an explicit no-objection certificate (NOC) for the proposal as part of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) approval process. The RBI is also likely to weigh longer-term prospects: if the merged businesses are later demerged to attract outside investment or an IPO, Tata Sons would revert to NBFC-CIC status.
Shapoorji Pallonji Group
The largest minority shareholder in Tata Sons, the Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group, has long advocated a listing to unlock value. Scrapping the prospect of an IPO could prompt SP to challenge the restructuring before the NCLT as oppressive to them.
Tata Cos’ vote might be key
The Trusts collectively own 66% of Tata Sons, but SRTT with 24% cannot currently vote on the merger because of the regulatory restriction. That makes Tata companies, which hold 13%, pivotal as the resolution requires 75% of shareholders to approve it. Their stance is unclear, and they are led by Chandrasekaran. If Tata companies and SP, which holds an 18% stake, both vote against, the restructuring resolution fails.

stories.headline: Benglauru couple pays Rs 1.4 lakh for premium suite, finds cockroaches on food, breast pump; hospital told to pay Rs 60,000
stories.deck: Shweta Pratap Jadhav and Anand Dubey chose Motherhood Hospital for their child's birth due to its reputation. They were disappointed by the presence of cockroaches and houseflies in their premium suite. After raising concerns, they were moved to another suite but remained dissatisfied with the response. The Bengaluru Urban district consumer disputes commission held the hospital responsible for…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A couple who chose a premium private suite for the birth of their child, hoping for hygienic and comfortable surroundings, instead found cockroaches and houseflies crawling across the room, including on their food and the breast pump used to feed their newborn. The III additional Bengaluru Urban district consumer disputes redressal commission has now held Motherhood Hospital liable for deficiency of service and ordered it to pay compensation for the ordeal.
The saga began when Shweta Pratap Jadhav, a resident of HSR Layout, and her husband Anand Dubey chose the Lullanagar branch of Motherhood Hospital in Pune for the delivery, as Jadhav's maternal home was in the city and the couple trusted the brand's reputation. She was admitted on Aug 21, 2024, and Dubey opted for a premium private suite at a cost of Rs 1.4 lakh, excluding medical expenses, to ensure the comfort and safety of the mother and child. However, the couple found the suite far below the promised standards.
Cockroaches and houseflies were spotted around 2am on the first night, on the floor, on the table with food items, and even the bed where Jadhav rested. Most alarmingly, pests were found on the breast pump being used for the newborn. 
When the couple raised the issue with hospital staff, they were shifted to another suite; however, they remained dissatisfied with the response. Dubey emailed the hospital on Dec 18, 2024, describing the family's traumatic experience. The hospital responded five days later, on Dec 23, seeking a meeting. The couple did not hear back until Jan 15, 2025. Alleging gross deficiency of service and unfair trade practice, they issued a legal notice. Disappointed with the response, they filed a consumer complaint on July 29, 2025, seeking a refund of Rs 1,43,518, compensation of Rs 20 lakh and litigation costs.
The hospital claimed Jadhav had raised concerns about the room shortly after admission and was immediately offered alternative rooms, with the staff extending full assistance. It said sanitation teams were instructed to conduct hourly checks, and gel-based preventive measures were applied as a precaution. The hospital maintained that Jadhav was discharged in healthy condition on Aug 23, 2024, had expressed satisfaction with her overall experience, and that the couple had approached the commission with malicious intent.
During proceedings, the family produced a pen drive containing videos showing cockroaches inside the suite. The hospital did not dispute the recordings. After considering the evidence and hearing both sides, the commission noted that the recordings supported the couple's case. The forum observed that failure to maintain hygienic conditions in a maternity hospital amounted to deficiency of service. "It is the bounden duty of the hospital to maintain hygienic conditions," the commission observed.
The commission declined to refund the suite charges, noting that adequate medical care was provided and there were no health complications. It, however, ordered Motherhood Hospital to pay Rs 50,000 for mental agony and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.

stories.headline: Why private schools in Karnataka are up for sale
stories.deck: Private schools in Karnataka are facing significant challenges, leading to many being put up for sale. As admissions decline, many schools struggle with operational costs and maintenance. Larger corporate schools are expanding into smaller towns, intensifying competition for existing schools. Additionally, family-run schools are exiting as new generations show less interest in managing…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Private schools in Karnataka are on sale. Dismissed as a one-off distress sale induced by Covid admission inertia, the whole school set-up, along with land and infrastructure, going on sale is becoming more common now, with at least 200 functional schools up for grabs, according to educationists and real estate agents specialising in educational properties.
Most of these are standalone, self-sustaining schools affiliated to state or central boards, which are finding it difficult to operate with thin margins and thinner admissions. Since infrastructure upgrades and faculty salaries are eating into their budget, managements are making a quiet exit, handing over the reins to professionally run schools, which are keen on expanding their footprint into smaller towns.
Business interactions are currently of three kinds: outright sale with land and infrastructure running into crores; rental or lease agreement ranging from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 40 lakh a month; and the profit-sharing model.
Corporate schools, which have reached near saturation growth in urban centres, are looking at smaller towns for expansion. "It's akin to kirana shops taken over by supermarkets," said Prasanna Kumar BG, founder and CEO, Edproperty, a real estate portal exclusively for educational properties.
Prasanna claimed around 200 schools are on sale. TOI couldn't independently verify the numbers since no exact data on this is fully computed so far.
Some schools unable to pay maintenance: KAMS secy Prasanna said: "State board schools - operating on smaller premises, with low fee structure - are seeing parents shift their children to bigger schools, especially into CBSE/ICSE curriculum. At the same time, smaller CBSE/ICSE schools are unable to face competition dictated by big brands entering their jurisdiction."
Agreed N Prabhakar Urs, founder of The School Company, which is into sale, rental and lease of schools. "Every corporate school is coming to district headquarters, creating tough competition for small, budget schools. They invest crores of rupees in one go. They have marketing strategies, offer admission-fee waivers, and other offers to attract parents. Their school buses ply up to 50km whereas that of a small school might ply for 15km. They pump in money for infrastructure and branding," he said.
On the other hand, state board schools are struggling with renewal-of-recognition compliances as the department is very stringent with them. Last year, around 5,500 schools in Karnataka did not receive renewals. Family-run schools are also on the block. "The next generation is not interested because this is not glamorous. It's not easy dealing with everyday problems like complaints from parents, teachers and so on. So the new generation is not inclined to stay with the business," Prasanna added.
D Shashi Kumar, secretary of Management of Primary and Secondary Schools of Karnataka, said Covid was a beginning. "With the dipping population, admissions to kindergarten have decreased across schools, irrespective of the management. Costs have escalated. Some schools with 100-200 students are not able to manage maintenance and are paying out of their pockets. They are all exiting business now," he said.
Shashi Kumar said real estate is the main driver in cities like Bengaluru. "Many investors are now no more educationists. They might be keen on investing in real estate property," he said.
"With newer curriculums, options for parents have widened. National Institute of Open Schooling, for instance, has been having a large patronage now," said a city school principal.
Many schools have not been able to sell because they come with a lot of liabilities. Some schools have invested heavily expecting good admissions but they don't. These liabilities include loans, court cases and lack of clarity over documents. "Nobody wants to get into that whirlpool. That is why many of them have not been sold," said the school principal.

stories.headline: BMRDA notifies new mobility road grid for Bengaluru Metropolitan Region
stories.bodyText:
The State government has notified a new mobility road grid for the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region (BMR), beyond the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) area, in an attempt to prevent problems that arise due to unplanned development from recurring in the fast-urbanising areas surrounding it.
This comes on the heels of the Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board’s footprint being expanded to include all of the Bengaluru Urban district.
Most of the roads notified now are brownfield roads, widening small village roads and other key roads to accommodate more traffic. The notification was issued under the Revised Bengaluru Structure Plan-2031 by the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA).
“The new notification covers hundreds of roads, including existing zilla panchayat, PWD, and State Highway roads that have been proposed for widening. Roads that were previously as narrow as 10 metres have been notified for widths of 30 metres, 45 metres and, in some cases, up to 90 metres. These roads have been notified as Comprehensive Development Plan roads in a grid pattern to support planned urban expansion,” said Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda on Tuesday.
Rajendra Cholan, Metropolitan Commissioner, BMRDA, said this was the first time a mobility grid exercise was conducted, following a drone survey of the area to assess gaps in the road network. “Most of these are brownfield roads being widened. Village roads connecting to district roads, roads connecting to the Peripheral Ring Road, Satellite Township Ring Road and other such major corridors will be widened to 30 metres, even up to 45 metres,” he said, adding, “For instance, there was a gap in connectivity between Anekal and Hoskote; that road stretch of around 40 kms will be developed now. Other key roads like Chapparakallu Road and IVC Road, which are key link roads, will be developed,” he said.
The grid plan also includes developing integrated freight hubs and intermodal transport hubs at all major towns surrounding Bengaluru, a proposed monorail, metro and bus rapid transport corridors.
In phases
Various government bodies working under the BMR would take up these road projects over the coming years. Mr. Gowda said complete construction of the identified road network could take five to ten years. “Given that the identified road network runs into thousands of kilometres, it will not be possible to construct all the roads simultaneously. The departments concerned have therefore been directed to take up the roads in phases and based on priority,” he said.
Restrictions on development
Mr. Gowda on Tuesday appealed to the people not to construct buildings or develop layouts along these alignments. “Land required for the notified road corridors will have to be left vacant while undertaking new layouts or constructing houses in these areas, in accordance with the applicable legal provisions,” he said.
Details to be put out
Mr. Gowda said that officials have also been directed to prepare and upload videos showing the existing and proposed road alignments on the BMRDA website.
“The BMRDA, zilla panchayat, and PWD officials have also been directed to jointly identify the notified roads and display the details on gram panchayat and Revenue Department notice boards,” he said.

stories.headline: BMTC to introduce automatic passenger counting system on 30 buses
stories.deck: The initiative is expected to give BMTC a more detailed picture of passenger demand across routes and trips
stories.bodyText:
The Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) is set to introduce an Automatic Passenger Counting (APC) system on 30 selected buses to obtain more accurate data on passenger movement, occupancy, and boarding and alighting patterns.
The system is intended to provide BMTC with automated information on the number of passengers boarding and alighting at different stops, along with onboard occupancy. According to officials, the system will also enable the transport corporation to compare passenger counts recorded by the APC with data from its Electronic Ticketing Machines (ETMs), including information relating to students and pass holders.
The initiative is expected to give BMTC a more detailed picture of passenger demand across routes and trips. The data generated through the system can be used for service planning, schedule rationalisation, analysing passenger loads, and identifying instances of overcrowding, officials said.
Passenger trends
“The APC system will be installed at passenger doors and will use sensors and onboard equipment to automatically detect passenger movement. The proposed solution will also include software and backend systems to process the data generated by the devices,” an official explained.
As part of the project, BMTC has called for a tender seeking a system that can provide passenger data by route, vehicle, trip and stop, as well as across different time periods. The system is also expected to provide dashboards, analytical tools and downloadable reports, allowing the corporation to examine passenger trends and operational data.
An important component of the project will be the integration of the APC system with BMTC’s existing technology infrastructure. The tender specifies that the solution should support integration with the corporation’s Automatic Vehicle Location System (AVLS), ETM system and other systems wherever required and where the necessary interfaces and data are made available by BMTC.
According to officials, the proposed system is expected to help BMTC independently verify passenger numbers recorded through its ticketing system. This could be particularly useful for understanding ridership on services where passengers travel using different categories of passes, as the APC data can provide an additional source of passenger movement information.
95% accuracy
The tender also specifies that the APC system should achieve a counting accuracy of at least 95% during commissioning. The passenger counts will be checked against corresponding ETM passenger data as part of the verification process. The successful service provider will also be required to undertake calibration and corrections based on observations made during acceptance testing.
Another senior BMTC official said the system may also help identify revenue leakage arising from two major issues: pilferage by employees and ticketless passengers travelling without paying fares.
“At present, checking inspectors penalise ticketless passengers and recommend disciplinary action against conductors found involved in corrupt practices. However, the corporation has been unable to effectively control pilferage. This system may help us identify and address these issues more effectively,” the official added.

briefs.headline: 200 people, 5 km, after 9 pm: Bengaluru walks after dark, confronts women’s safety
briefs.bodyText:
Last Sunday, at 9.30pm, around 200 people, mostly women, gathered in Koramangala to walk five kilometres to Indiranagar along the Intermediate Ring Road, demanding greater safety for women in public spaces after dark. The route, which included poorly lit stretches and isolated patches, was chosen deliberately to draw attention to the spaces many women hesitate to navigate at night.
The Bengaluru march was part of a nationwide mobilisation in solidarity with student protests in Delhi after a 17-year-old reported being gang-raped by three men allegedly posing as police officers. Another incident that shook the country took place in Bihar’s Jamui the previous week, where a Class 10 student and her male friend were assaulted by a group of men. Outrage also grew online and offline after colleges in Delhi asked women students to stay home citing safety concerns.
Minor acts of harassment can form part of a continuum that leads to more serious forms of violence. We have to start voicing our opinion even if it’s the smallest form of sexual harassment. Let the world see and let the predators know that they are under scrutiny
Sneha, participant
For theatre practitioner, poet and organiser Nupur Saraswat, the march grew out of her involvement with the ‘Why Loiter’ campaign, which has previously organised walks challenging restrictions on women’s access to public spaces after dark. Like earlier walks, the Bengaluru march began at 9.30pm, questioning the idea that streets become off-limits to women after a certain hour. 
“One of the banners at the protest summed up the sentiment: A man’s day is 24 hours and a woman’s day is 14 hours,” she says.
Men must actively ensure that they do not make women uncomfortable in public spaces. All you can do, is not be the problem
Anuj, participant
It is shocking to note that as the group made its way along the Intermediate Ring Road, several women were catcalled and heckled by men. “In the end, the point of the walk was made by doing the walk,” says Nupur. The experience, she adds, offered a firsthand reminder of why women can feel unsafe in public spaces, even when moving through them as part of a large group.
Even during this protest march, several women were catcalled and heckled by men. In the end, the point of the walk was made by doing the walk
Nupur Saraswat, organiser
For Sneha*, a fitness coach who participated in the march, one of its most striking aspects was hearing people share their own experiences. “We had a few pit stops where we stood and shared our stories. So many people came forward with their experiences of harassment and assault, and some even spoke about how it had happened within their own families,” she says. The conversations reinforced the reason behind the march, she says: women continue to feel unsafe not only at night or in public spaces, but also during the day and even within their own homes.
For Nupur, the marches serve as a reminder that such incidents are not isolated events that matter only when they make national headlines. They also tell women that they are not alone, while encouraging people to remain vigilant and speak up about what happens in their immediate surroundings.
* Name changed on request.

briefs.headline: Still charging: Bengaluru’s BDA apartments yet to fully turn EV infra switch on
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 With electric vehicle (EV) adoption shifting into the fast lane as more and more households own or shift to them, charging infrastructure is at the centre of discussions in apartment complexes. Among Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) apartment projects, only one of the 15 complexes surveyed in Aug had an operational community EV-charging facility.
BDA Apartment Owners’ Forum conducted the survey across its 15 properties to assess demand and readiness for EV charging infrastructure. The two-level survey, which covered 5,000 flats, found that 61% of residents already owned an EV. Two-wheelers made up most of this: 70% of EV-owning households had only an electric two-wheeler, 20% had both a two-wheeler and a four-wheeler, and 10% had only a four-wheeler.
Since community charging was largely missing, residents were found to be managing on their own. Some 41% of them used public or commercial charging stations, 28% charged at home, and 17% charged at the workplace. Only 11% had a dedicated charger at their own parking spot — exposing a huge gap between what residents need and what is available.
In response to the survey, a senior BDA official told 
TOI
: “All apartments will have EV-charging stations. BDA is leading the effort to convert vehicles to EVs, and we will do everything possible towards this. 
The chairperson has asked us to take up EV-charging projects in existing apartments as well.”
The survey found strong interest among those who don’t yet own an EV. All of them said they were planning to buy one in the next two years. Interestingly, more of these future buyers want four-wheelers, which need stronger charging setups than the two-wheelers most residents currently own. The forum said this should be kept in mind while planning charging infrastructure for the future.
Residents said the survey indicates that EV adoption is already gaining traction across BDA apartment communities. However, the lack of adequate charging infrastructure remains a key challenge.
A member of BDA Apartment Owners’ Forum said: “The survey aimed to identify gaps in EV infrastructure and understand how they can be addressed to encourage wider adoption of electric vehicles. We believe the authority can play a key role by improving EV infrastructure and facilitating necessary approvals, particularly for projects that remain under its control. This would make it easier for more residents to shift to EVs.”
Their broader goal was to help BDA apartment communities evolve into better, more convenient and future-ready places to live, on a par with leading residential communities.
Non-Owner Pipeline Findings
* Non-owners considering EV purchase: 100%
* Purchase timeline (6 months – 1 year): 40%
* Purchase timeline (not fixed): 32%
* Likely type — four-wheeler: 56%
* Likely type — two-wheeler: 37%
EV Ownership & Vehicle Mix
* Residents who already own an EV: 61%
* Households with 1 EV: 62%
* Households with 2 EVs: 32%
* Households with 3+ EVs: 6%
* Electric 2-wheeler only: 70%
* Both 2 & 4-wheelers: 20%
* Electric 4-wheeler only: 10%
Charging Behaviour & Challenges
* Charging via public/commercial: 41%
* Via regular home socket: 28%

briefs.headline: Patch-up time: Minister sets 15-day deadline to identify critical roads on Bengaluru’s outskirts
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Thousands of residents living in the city’s rapidly urbanising outskirts could finally see some long-awaited infrastructure improvements, with Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda directing officials to identify critical road stretches in peripheral areas that have remained neglected despite witnessing significant growth.
Gowda said the public works department (PWD), Bengaluru Urban district administration, and Bengaluru Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA) have been given 15 days to prepare a list of roads in poor condition outside the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) limits, particularly those bordering GBA, so they can be taken up on priority.
The move comes amid growing concerns over infrastructure in several developing corridors where residential layouts, apartment complexes and commercial establishments have mushroomed over the years, but road infrastructure has failed to keep pace.
The issue has been a long-standing concern in several fringe areas. A couple of days ago, 
TOI
 reported on the condition of Doddamara Road, which has remained non-motorable for nearly a decade, with residents alleging that repeated appeals to authorities yielded little response. Similar concerns have been raised from rapidly developing localities in Sarjapur, Mullur, Anekal and other peripheral areas struggling with inadequate road infrastructure.
Many of these localities, though closely linked to Bengaluru’s urban growth, fall outside GBA limits and are often caught between multiple agencies, resulting in delayed infrastructure works and poor maintenance. Residents have frequently complained that civic amenities have failed to keep pace with the speed of development.
Acknowledging the challenge, Gowda said authorities have been tasked with conducting a ground-level assessment to identify road stretches where deteriorating conditions are affecting mobility and daily life.
“From the current 740sqkm GBA area, urbanisation has already spread to nearly 1,200sqkm around Bengaluru. The growth has been so rapid that providing adequate infrastructure has become a challenge. We agree that govts shouldn’t match up to the rapid urbanisation...now that I’ve taken PWD also on board, we will try to fix these infrastructure gaps at the earliest,” Gowda said.
According to the minister, the exercise is intended as an immediate intervention to identify roads that require urgent attention and prepare them for priority repairs and upgrades.
Officials said the assessment is expected to cover several growth corridors surrounding Bengaluru that have witnessed rapid urbanisation in recent years. Once the survey is completed, a priority list will be prepared for infrastructure improvements, offering relief to residents who have long argued that road development has lagged behind the city’s expansion.

briefs.headline: Newborn’s body found in bag near lake in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A driver made a grim discovery near Agara Lake in HSR Layout Sunday morning when he found a bag left by the roadside and opened it to see the body of a newborn boy.
Maruthi
, a mini-goods vehicle driver from Ramamurthynagar, told police he had parked his vehicle near Agara Lake around 7.30am and went towards the waterbody with friend Sharanabasava to relieve themselves. They noticed a bag lying nearby, with what appeared to be a baby’s leg protruding through an opening.
On checking, Maruthi found blood on the leg and realised it was a newborn. It had been wrapped in a bedsheet and placed in the bag. He suspected the baby was already dead and called police helpline 112.
A Hoysala patrolling team confirmed the baby was dead. HSR Layout police subsequently shifted the body to the mortuary for further examination and to ascertain the cause of death.
A case has been registered under BNS Section 94 (concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body) of BNS based on Maruthi’s complaint. Police are trying to identify the baby’s parents or those responsible for abandoning him.

briefs.headline: IIM Bangalore alumni raise Rs 20 lakh for injured student
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The Indian Institute of Management Bangalore Alumni Association (IIMBAA) community raised Rs over 20.1 lakh to support a student who was seriously injured in an 
accident
.
The student met with the accident on Aug 15 and was admitted to Fortis Hospital, Bannerghatta Road, in a coma. An appeal for financial assistance was shared with the alumni community on Sept 25, with an initial fundraising target of Rs 18 lakh.
Within two hours, the target was met. By the end of the campaign, 267 alumni had contributed Rs 20.11 lakh, while many others amplified the appeal within their networks and reached out to fellow alumni to mobilise support, said a release from the association.
“I am proud to see IIMBAA becoming a real community, one where people come together to help each other when it matters. Our job was to reduce the family’s hardships, at least the financial part, as they struggle to deal with the trauma,” said Harish Mittal (PGP ’88), president, IIMBAA.
The student is currently out of ICU and is at the rehab centre of the hospital.

briefs.headline: Govt notifies future road corridors as Bengaluru eyes expansion
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 In a bid to prevent unplanned urbanisation from choking future infrastructure projects, the state govt is set to notify a network of proposed road corridors in rapidly developing areas outside Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) area, asking residents and developers to verify designated alignments before undertaking new construction.
Announcing the move Tuesday, Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda said the notification aims to safeguard land required for future road widening and Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP) roads under the Revised Master Plan, as Bengaluru expands beyond its current limits.
Govt has identified roads connecting taluk headquarters, hobli centres, district roads, state highways, Peripheral Ring Road and Satellite Town Ring Road as part of a larger road grid planned for Bengaluru’s future growth corridors.
While details on the total number and length of roads were not immediately available, Gowda said maps of the corridors, along with video documentation of their present condition, would be uploaded on the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA) website.
Officials estimate Bengaluru’s urban footprint, currently around 750sqkm, could expand to between 1,400sqkm and 1,800sqkm as development spreads into surrounding areas. 
Gowda said nearly 110 villages were earlier brought into the city’s limits without adequate infrastructure planning, making subsequent acquisition of land for roads, water supply and drainage difficult and expensive.
“Whether we like it or not, urbanisation around Bengaluru is inevitable. If we don’t plan now, the same problems being faced within Bengaluru today will be repeated on the city’s outskirts tomorrow,” he said.
The minister said govt had moved to protect land earmarked for future road widening and CDP roads before large-scale development takes place. According to drone surveys conducted by the authorities, nearly 90% of the land required for the proposed corridors remains greenfield, while about 10% has witnessed development.
According to Gowda, landowners would be required to leave space earmarked for roads and could use the remaining portion for construction and development. He urged landowners, builders and prospective homebuyers to consult the notified plans on the BMRDA website before undertaking projects.
The notification will cover hundreds of roads, many proposed to be widened from existing widths of around 10 metres to 30 metres, 45 metres and, in some cases, up to 90 metres. Development of the network is expected to take place in phases over the coming years, but officials said notifying the corridors now would help secure land needed for Bengaluru’s future infrastructure.

briefs.headline: This Bengaluru-based music ensemble brings the poetry of Kabirdas to modern audiences
briefs.deck: The Sadho Project is set to perform Songs of the Seeker, revolving around Kabirdas’ poetry, on September 30
briefs.bodyText:
“This project began as an experiment to bring together sounds from around the world,” says Vivaswath Rao, founder of The Sadho Project. “We take inspiration from nature, the sounds of flowing rivers and chirping birds.” . The group is scheduled to perform Songs of the Seeker at Bangalore International Centre on September 30. It is an experimental and immersive musical exploration of Kabirdas’ poetry.
The Sadho Project is a Bengaluru-based music quintet which was established in July 2025, and their work focuses on the philosophy and poetry of Kabirdas, but in a slightly different light, Vivaswath says. In their performances, Indian folk instruments meet modern-day electronic textures and percussion, making their take on bhajans and poetry experimental. Its members include Vivaswath, singer and composer Roopini Ravindran, singer Kusumitha Vasanth, pianist Aditi Bharatee and multi-instrument percussionist Anirudh Sharma.
The 90-minute event will have Kabir’s timeless poetry, blended with folk instruments, sounds from nature, electronic textures and unexpected percussion. Audiences are welcome to listen, reflect and sing along to well-known couplets and become seekers for an evening.
When asked what made them choose this poet in particular, Kusumitha says, “Kabir’s poetry is still relevant. What he said centuries ago will never stop being relevant. The metaphors he used are relatable even today.” The group bridges his works’ timeless antiquity and contemporary modernity through their performances.
Roopini, who also manages their sound effects, says, “We try to recreate his world of poetry and philosophy in a more immersive form. We don’t add or alter the original works in any way, but rather work towards bringing out the nuances of his poetry through sound and music.”
Being a five-member band adds to their production expertise. Anirudh says, “We make it a point to meet quite frequently, to discuss poetry, music and instruments. We have the freedom of adding our own elements to it. I feel we all get the space to express ourselves.”
Each of the singers and instrumentalists come from musical backgrounds that include Indian classical music, Western music, orchestration, harmonies and more, and their combined effort makes The Sadho Project unique.
“We take inspiration from folk music and work with electronic sounds. All of this comes together in our songs,” says Roopini. Aditi says, “We do not hesitate to try different things such as poetry recitation with singing. For some compositions Anirudh plays two tablas with different pitches. We try to keep an open mind about where our experimentation takes us.”
Vivaswath believes that one has to experience the performance firsthand to find their own interpretation or takeaway message. Post performance, the artistes will interact with the audiences.
Songs of the Seeker will be presented on September 30, from 7pm at Bangalore International Centre. Entry free. For details visit bangaloreinternationalcentre.org or @thesadhoproject on Instagram

stories.headline: OpenAI unveils GPT-6.1 Sol and ‘Dots’ AI agents at DevDay
stories.deck: Sam Altman unveils lower-cost model at DevDay as OpenAI showcases always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra
stories.bodyText:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) unveiled GPT-6.1 Sol at the company’s DevDay conference in San Francisco, positioning it as a lower-cost model that delivers “very near-Astra-level intelligence at a fifth of the price” for coding and building. Mr. Altman said the model offers a balance of cost and capability and would make it cheaper for agents to reuse context, iterate on solutions and work through longer tasks. He said Sol was “smarter than Astra in some ways” and would become a “daily workhorse”.
OpenAI’s developer documentation says GPT-6.1 Sol is designed to offer a trade-off between capability and cost. The model is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while supporting reasoning levels from low to maximum. It has a 1.05-million-token context window and can generate up to 128,000 tokens in a response.
The model supports tools including web search, file search, code interpretation, hosted shell, computer use, image generation, skills and Model Context Protocol (MCP). It can be accessed through OpenAI’s Responses API, with function calling and structured outputs also supported.
OpenAI also launched UltraFast across its API, ChatGPT and Codex. Mr. Altman said it can reach 300 tokens a second, with eight times the speed and six times the price of the standard offering. UltraFast is available with Astra and will soon be offered with GPT-6.1 Sol.
At DevDay, OpenAI also showcased Dots, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra. The company says Dots have their own cloud computers, can connect to more than 4,000 applications and can work across multiple projects without requiring users to direct every step. They can be accessed through ChatGPT, Slack and Microsoft Teams.
OpenAI is also beginning enterprise pilots of specialist Dots, which can have their own identities, credentials and access to company systems to perform defined responsibilities. The company said it is working with Microsoft to integrate the agents with governance and security controls in Agent 365.
The announcements come a day after OpenAI confirmed that it had shelved GPT-6.1 Astra, which had been planned for an October release. The Wall Street Journal reported that internal testing found the model did not meet the company’s safety and alignment standards, citing problems including staying within authorised scope and accurately communicating actions to users. Reuters reported that OpenAI confirmed the decision.
In his closing remarks, Mr. Altman said he found the description of AI as a new industrial revolution “quite off-putting”, arguing that its best version should not be about making people “cogs in a giant machine”. Some parts of life, he said, “cannot and should not” be automated. If developed correctly, he said, AI could instead usher in “a new renaissance”, giving people more power over their own lives and more tools to create, learn, discover and expand knowledge.
