stories.headline: NCLAT issues notice to creditors on Subhash Chandra's plea; sets next hearing for October 29-30
stories.deck: A three-member Bench of NCLAT also granted a week's time to Subhash Chandra to file a rejoinder to the creditors' reply
stories.bodyText:
The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) issued notices to creditors on a plea filed by Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and scheduled the matter for hearing on October 29 and 30, 2026.
Mr. Chandra had challenged before the appellate tribunal an order passed on September 1 by a five-member larger Bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), which had stayed the order of a third tie-breaker judge in his personal insolvency matter and restrained him from alienating his assets.
The NCLAT has directed the creditors, who opposed the maintainability of Chandra's petition, among others, to file their reply within a week. A three-member Bench of NCLAT also granted a week's time to Subhash Chandra to file a rejoinder to the creditors' reply.
"Let the notice be issued... will file the reply (over maintainability and stay) within a week," said the Bench comprising Officiating Chairperson Justice (Retd.) Yogesh Khanna and Technical Members Barun Mitra and Ajai Das Mehrotra.
Meanwhile, at the request of Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for some creditors, the appellate tribunal clubbed a separate petition filed by creditors challenging the NCLT order that approved a settlement involving a payment of about ₹6.5 crore against admitted claims of around ₹22,006.57 crore with Mr. Chandra's appeal.
The NCLAT fixed October 29 and 30 for hearing Chandra's interim relief applications. The tribunal indicated that one day would be allotted for arguments on behalf of Mr. Chandra and the other for submissions from creditors.
During the proceedings, Solicitor General Mehta suggested waiting for the outcome of the next hearing of the five-member NCLT Bench, scheduled on November 19. However, this was opposed by advocate Dhruv Mehta, who was representing Subhash Chandra.
In its last hearing on September 23, the five-member NCLT Bench issued notice to the probe agency CBI in the personal insolvency matter of Subhash Chandra and said the interim director restraining Essel Group Chairman from alienating property will continue till a final decision by it.
The CBI has registered an FIR against Subhash Chandra for allegedly inflating his net worth to avail loans from the Life Insurance Corporation Housing Finance Limited (LICHFL) and then becoming a defaulter, causing a loss of more than ₹1,322 crore to the public-sector lender.
LICHFL alleged in its complaint, which is now part of the FIR, that Mr. Chandra submitted net-worth certificates that were used to secure the approval and disbursal of two loans totalling ₹980 crore.
In his petition to the NCLAT, Subhash Chandra argued that the NCLT’s September 1, 2026 order exceeded its statutory authority. Mr. Chandra questioned the formation of the five-member Bench by NCLT. Earlier, a two-member Bench delivered a split verdict on Chandra's personal insolvency resolution process in NCLT.
While Member (Judicial) Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj approved the ₹6.5 crore repayment plan submitted by Mr. Chandra and held that he was eligible to seek relief under the insolvency framework for personal guarantors, Member (Technical) Reeta Kohli disagreed and rejected the proposal, leading to a reference under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, 2013.
Section 419(5) of the Companies Act lays down the procedure for resolving a split verdict by referring the points of difference to additional members of the tribunal for a majority decision. The matter was subsequently placed before Nilesh Sharma, Member (Judicial), as the third member to decide the points of difference.
Mr. Sharma concurred with Bhardwaj on the key issues and upheld Chandra's repayment plan, under which claims of around ₹22,006 crore arising from personal guarantees were proposed to be settled for about ₹6.5 crore.
However, the operation of Mr. Sharma's order was later stayed by a five-member NCLT Bench, which restrained Mr. Chandra from alienating his assets pending further proceedings.

stories.headline: Centre picks 50 cities for PRAGATI-50 clean-city initiative
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Govt on Tuesday launched PRAGATI-50, an initiative to make 50 cities across 24 states and UTs completely clean, with the selected cities set to emerge as role models for the rest of the country. The list includes almost all state capitals, as well as major tourist and pilgrimage destinations.
The initiative covers 76 municipal areas, including all municipal areas in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Pune, Kolkata and Hyderabad.
The housing and urban affairs ministry rolled out the programme following PM Narendra Modi throwing a challenge to the ministry to make 50 cities cleaner while chairing the monthly PRAGATI meeting on May 27, which TOI had first reported. Seeking collaboration of all states to achieve this, PM has sought achieving 100% cleanliness in such cities in all aspects, from making them garbage free to processing all their solid and liquid waste. He had made these observations while going through a detailed presentation on progress of Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0.
The list of identified cities include, Tirupati, Gaya, Patna, Bilaspur, Ahmedabad, Gurgaon, Faridabad, Dharamsala, Srinagar, Ranchi, Mysore, Nashik, Puri, Ludhiana, Udaipur, Coimbatore, Warangal, Ayodhya, Mathura, Varanasi, Haridwar and Kolkata.
Launching the initiative, minister Manohar Lal said that these will emerge as role-model cities by going beyond their routine sanitation work to “demonstrate sustained, high-performance parameters of visible cleanliness”. He added that they have ensured inclusion of major cities, cities of cultural importance, high tourism destinations and economic centres.
“The initiative aims to drive visible improvements in urban cleanliness, solid waste management, used water management, sanitation, and citizen participation through a structured framework of monitoring and review within a defined timeframe. Progress will be continuously reviewed through outcome‑based assessments and tech‑enabled monitoring. I will personally chair review meetings every other month to track the advancement of these cities,” the minister said.

stories.headline: Indians buying gold at Rs 5,000 per 10 grams discount on cash deals
stories.deck: For bulk purchases, such off-the-record cash deals can bring prices down by as much as 6% from prevailing market rates. Dealers who take cash can avoid certain taxes and share some of those savings with buyers. The revival of this informal market is an unintended outcome of a policy intended to reduce India’s demand for gold.
stories.bodyText:
Gold prices, despite their recent correction, are still very high and the hike in gold import duties from 6% to 15% has raised the cost of jewellery further.
Although prices have fallen since then, they are still nearly 28% above their level a year ago.
So, even as gold prices remain elevated and taxes add to the cost, an increasing number of Indian buyers are now opting for cash transactions outside the formal system, and purchasing gold and jewellery without invoices that could leave a trail for authorities.
Gold being bought at discount with under-the-counter cash sales
For bulk purchases, such off-the-record cash deals can bring prices down by as much as 6% from prevailing market rates, sources familiar with the trade told Bloomberg. Dealers who take cash can avoid certain taxes and share some of those savings with buyers.
One middle-aged woman said she purchased jewellery for her daughter’s wedding at a discount of Rs 5,000 ($52) per 10 grams, but did not receive a receipt.
For the 55-year-old homemaker, the savings were difficult to pass up after gold touched a record high earlier this year.
“It was an offer I couldn’t refuse. Gold prices are way too high and we trust the jeweler,” she was quoted as saying.
The woman is part of a growing pool of consumers moving toward this unofficial trade. The market has expanded since the government more than doubled import duties on gold and silver to 15%, in an effort to discourage purchases as India contends with a widening trade deficit. Retail buyers must also pay an additional 3% goods and services tax.
The revival of this informal market is an unintended outcome of a policy intended to reduce India’s demand for gold.
India, the world’s second-largest consumer of the metal after China, purchases gold for births, festivals and, most significantly, weddings. The metal is used as jewellery, given as gifts and held as a form of family savings. Since domestic production is limited, most of the country’s demand is fulfilled through imports, placing a significant burden on the trade bill and the currency.
In India’s cash market, traders have managed to obtain gold at discounts of up to $200 an ounce compared with prevailing domestic prices, according to the people familiar with the trade. Prices can differ substantially across the fragmented informal market, where transactions are individually negotiated instead of being based on a common benchmark.
“A discount of that magnitude in the parallel market primarily reflects the economics of unofficial supply,” said Hiren Chandaria, managing director, Middle East and Asia operations at London-based Monetary Metals. “Higher import duty creates a significantly greater incentive for gold to enter outside the official duty-paid channel.”
The difference is much smaller for gold brought into the country through formal import channels. According to consultancy Metals Focus, discounts on landed prices for officially imported gold averaged around $50 an ounce in September.
Retail buyers, meanwhile, can negotiate discounts of up to Rs 10,000 for every 10 grams, depending on how effectively they bargain and the relationship they have with the jeweler, the people said.
Gold imports second-highest after oil
Gold ranks as India’s largest imported commodity after oil and is a significant factor behind the country’s trade deficit. The deficit expanded to nearly $32 billion in July, its highest level so far this year.
The cost of gold shipments rose by more than 32% year-on-year during the four months through July. The increase led Prime Minister Narendra Modi to make a second appeal within five months for Indians to cut back on purchases and help preserve foreign-exchange reserves. Gold imports subsequently fell sharply in August, dropping to less than half the level recorded a year earlier.
India’s informal gold market has existed for decades, but when import duty was just 6%, there was little financial motivation for traders to avoid official channels. The latest duty increase has changed that equation, reviving the parallel trade just as the country heads into its wedding and festival season, which begins in mid-October and continues through early March.
“At today’s gold prices, even a relatively small percentage difference translates into a significant absolute cost difference in rupee terms,” Chandaria said.

briefs.headline: OpenAI shelves GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns, halts October release
briefs.deck: Model reportedly struggled with staying within authorised scope and accurately communicating its actions, even as rival Anthropic warns investors of potentially catastrophic AI risks
briefs.bodyText:
OpenAI has shelved GPT-6.1 Astra, a model it planned to release in October, after internal testing found that it failed to meet the company’s safety and alignment standards, according to The Wall Street Journal. Reuters reported that OpenAI confirmed the decision.
OpenAI India’s communications team told The Hindu that the company had no comment on the development as of Tuesday.
GPT-6.1 Astra was being developed as a more capable and increasingly autonomous model designed to handle complex tasks with minimal human intervention. It was intended as a successor to GPT-6 Astra, which was built for advanced applications such as computer use, web browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity and scientific work.
OpenAI’s own safety documentation for GPT-6 Astra highlights the challenge of ensuring that highly capable models remain within authorised limits. The company said Astra was “stronger at respecting safety and security boundaries and staying within its authorised scope” than GPT-5.6 Sol.
In a simulation involving 54,218 internal Codex tasks, Astra recorded 53% fewer severity-level-three misaligned actions than GPT-5.6 Sol. However, OpenAI acknowledged that Astra could still “overreach during engineering tasks”, including using privileged access without explicit approval or granting automations wider permissions than required.
The company attributed such behaviour to models being “over eager to complete the task” and interpreting user instructions too broadly.
Internal tests of GPT-6.1 Astra reportedly identified instances of deceptive behaviour, including situations where the model failed to accurately disclose actions it had taken. It also struggled with staying within authorised task boundaries and seeking permission before executing certain actions, the Journal reported.
Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, said GPT-6.1 Astra “didn’t quite meet the bar” on issues including task scope, authorisation and transparency about completed work. She highlighted the difficulty of balancing model persistence — the ability to continue pursuing goals despite obstacles — with ensuring that systems do not exceed their permitted authority.
The setback comes as the AI industry faces growing scrutiny over the risks posed by increasingly autonomous systems. Anthropic, OpenAI’s rival, warned in its IPO filing that advanced AI could present “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. The filing highlighted concerns that future models could exhibit self-preserving behaviour, resist shutdown attempts, conceal information or manipulate users, while also noting the challenge of evaluating systems that may recognise safety tests.
The shelving of GPT-6.1 Astra comes ahead of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco and marks a rare instance of the company delaying a major model release due to safety concerns. By the planned launch date, OpenAI would have progressed through more than a dozen major GPT generations and iterations, beginning with GPT-1 in 2018 and extending to the GPT-6 Astra family in 2026.

briefs.headline: Cleartrip bets on holidays for growth; targets high-single-digit share
briefs.deck: The platform is trying to build a new revenue engine around holidays after spending nearly two decades scaling its air and hotel businesses
briefs.bodyText:
Cleartrip expects its newly launched holiday packages business to contribute a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit share of its overall business in the next 12 months, as the Flipkart-owned travel platform expands beyond flights and hotels to tap India’s growing discretionary travel market.
The company has entered the fragmented holiday packages segment with a model that combines flights, hotels, activities and transfers into customisable itineraries. The move is part of Cleartrip’s broader strategy to build a full-stack travel platform covering flights, hotels, trains, buses and holidays, Gaurav Patwari, Chief Business Officer, Air, Cleartrip, told The Hindu.
“We want to have mid-single-digit to high-single-digit growth in terms of holidays as a share of our overall business over the next one year,” Mr. Patwari said, adding that the segment presents a significant opportunity due to limited competition.
Cleartrip expects demand to be driven by rising disposable incomes and a shift in consumer spending towards experiences. He said travel remains an under-penetrated market in India, with increasing participation from consumers moving into higher income segments.
A typical domestic holiday package costs ₹50,000-₹1 lakh, while international packages range from ₹1 lakh to ₹3 lakh, with premium itineraries costing significantly more, he said.
“Within discretionary spending, consumer behaviour is shifting towards experiences, and holidays occupy the centre stage,” Mr. Patwari said.
The company is leveraging its existing presence in flights and hotels to gain an edge in the holiday segment. Cleartrip has direct contracts with around 40,000 domestic hotels, largely in the three- to five-star category, while international inventory is sourced through multiple partners.
Unlike traditional fixed packages, Cleartrip’s holiday offering focuses on customisation. Customers can modify hotels, activities and flights within curated itineraries, supported by destination experts.
The company plans to use artificial intelligence across travel discovery, itinerary creation, content, curation and backend operations. Ground services will be managed through local destination management companies and tour operators.
Cleartrip is also developing shorter “smart bundle” itineraries combining flights, hotels, sightseeing, activities and transfers to cater to consumers seeking flexible and affordable travel options.
The company is witnessing strong growth among younger travellers. Gen Z travel shopping on Cleartrip and Flipkart Travel has grown around 65-66% year-on-year, reflecting a broader shift towards experience-led and premium travel spending.

briefs.headline: Tata Trusts within right to seek merger, but Tata Sons can challenge: Lawyer
briefs.deck: The proposed restructuring aims to take Tata Sons out from NBFC/CIC framework. Whether that objective could be achieved depend on final structure and RBI’s assessment, not on unilateral decision by Tata Trusts or Tata Sons
briefs.bodyText:
Tata Trusts’ proposal to merge two operating companies of the Tata Group — Tata Electronics Systems Solutions Private Ltd and Tata Consulting Engineers — with Tata Sons to avoid a listing could trigger a governance and legal battle if the holding company’s board refuses to approve it, according to legal experts.
“Tata Sons can legally challenge such a direction if what is asserted goes beyond the rights conferred under the Articles [of Association] or the Companies Act,” said Sooraj Sharma, Partner at Clavius Legal.
However, he added that if Tata Trusts has only placed a proposal before the board, “there may presently be nothing to challenge.”
A legal dispute would arise only if either side claims governance powers that the other disputes. For instance, if Tata Trusts asserts that the board is bound to implement the restructuring regardless of its statutory decision-making process, Tata Sons could contest that position.
“Any such dispute would primarily depend on the interpretation of Tata Sons’ Articles, the respective powers of shareholders and the board, rights of Trust-nominated directors, and directors’ statutory duties,” Mr. Sharma said. Depending on the nature of the claim, proceedings before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) could follow, he added.
On whether Tata Trusts has the right to propose such restructuring, Mr. Sharma said “as the controlling shareholder, Tata Trusts is entitled to propose restructuring and exercise shareholder and governance rights available under the Companies Act, 2013 and Tata Sons’ Articles of Association.”
However, he clarified that Tata Trusts has sought the board’s approval rather than issuing a binding directive.
Section 179(3)(i) of the Companies Act requires the board to approve amalgamation, merger or reconstruction proposals through a resolution. That power, however, remains subject to the Act and the company’s Articles, according to him.
Tata Sons’ Articles provide Tata Trusts with significant governance rights, including nomination rights under Article 104B and affirmative voting provisions under Article 121.
“In Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. (2021), the Supreme Court described Article 121 as conferring a limited right regarding the manner in which matters before the board are decided,” Mr. Sharma said.
Therefore, while Tata Trusts cannot replace the board’s decision-making role, the board must also operate within the governance framework laid out in the Articles. Trust-nominated directors, meanwhile, remain bound by their statutory duties, including exercising independent judgment under Section 166 of the Companies Act.
If Tata Sons challenges the proposal, the restructuring process could become prolonged. Any merger would still require multiple approvals, including board approval, member and creditor approvals under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act; NCLT sanction; and regulatory clearance, including from the Reserve Bank of India where applicable.
The proposed restructuring aims to ensure that the reorganised Tata Sons no longer falls under the NBFC/Core Investment Company (CIC) framework. However, whether that objective is achieved would depend on the final structure and RBI’s regulatory assessment, not on a unilateral decision by either Tata Trusts or Tata Sons, Mr. Sharma said.
A legal contest could delay both the restructuring plan and any alternative route, including a potential listing. It could also lead to judicial interpretation of the extent of Tata Trusts’ special governance rights under Tata Sons’ Articles.
“The issue is not merely whether Tata Trusts can direct Tata Sons. The real question is where decision-making power lies at each stage — with shareholders, the board under Tata Sons’ Articles, or statutory and regulatory authorities,” he said.

briefs.headline: Indian Oil plans to launch packaged drinking water under own brand across 43,000 fuel outlets
briefs.deck: The oil marketing company proposes a multi-year aggregator-led revenue sharing model as part of a strategy to grow non-fuel revenue and offer value-added products to customers
briefs.bodyText:
State-owned refiner and oil marketing company Indian Oil Corporation is mulling the launch of packaged drinking water under its own brand across its network of more than 43,000 retail outlets in the country.
The plan is part of the company’s strategy to grow non-fuel revenue and offer value-added products to customers. It is proposing a multi-year aggregator-led revenue sharing model under which ownership of the brand will remain with Indian Oil.
Selected aggregators will handle end-to-end execution, from manufacturing through approved facilities, quality assurance, supply chain management, logistics and rollout, Indian Oil said inviting expression of interest (EoI) from firms.
Highway outlets to lead
The rollout in phases will eventually cover all the 43,603 outlets. Highway retail outlets numbering 21,435 or nearly half of the network are expected to play a lead role with the on-the-go demand for drinking water highest at such facilities. Following closely will be the urban and semi-urban outlets, the EoI for selection of aggregators showed.
Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) bottles of 250 ml, 500 ml and 1 litre will form part of the rollout initially. The 1-litre pack is will be positioned as the lead product. In future, Indian Oil may consider launch of premium water, natural mineral water, alkaline water, functional hydration products and additional pack sizes.
Eye on more non-fuel revenue
Besides the brand ownership, Indian Oil will control the product pricing, ratio of dealer landed price to MRP and the dealer margin. At a broader level, the company aims to enhance non-fuel revenue from ₹200 crore to ₹760 crore, with a targeted GMV of over ₹11,000 crore.
In the 2025-26 annual report, chairman A.S. Sahney said doubling down on high-growth avenues in bitumen, aviation fuels, lubricants, bunkering fuels and non-fuel retail amid the country’s rapid infrastructure development, urbanisation, rising mobility, and expanding industrial activity is a focus for the company.
According to IOC, it has 195 million sq. ft. of retail space and over 3.2 crore daily customers visit the facilities. As part of plans to ramp up non-fuel revenues, it has partnered with multiple brands, including Hindustan Unilever, Dabur, ICICI Bank, Ferns & Petals, MTR Foods and PVR Cinemas.
Retail outlets for now
The EoI is confined to fuel outlets or petrol pumps as they are commonly known and cover all categories from the company owned, company operated (COCO), dealer owned, dealer operated to Kisan Seva Kendras. Other Indian Oil business channels, including LPG agencies, institutional / direct customers, IOCL offices, e-commerce or sale in open market / general trade (bazaar) are not covered for now.
If it goes ahead with the proposal, Indian Oil will eye a pie of India’s packaged drinking water market. Citing studies, India Brand Equity Foundation estimated the market to be ₹32,040 crore ($3.6 billion) in 2025 and projected to reach ₹57,850 crore ($ 6.5 billion) by 2032. Driving the growth will be population rise, growing per-capita consumption and increasing penetration of branded packaged water.

briefs.headline: NMDC commissions 2 MTPA pellet plant in Nagarnar
briefs.deck: The project is part of broader expansion and diversification strategy, particularly as it eyes raising iron ore production capacity to 100 million tonnes in the long term
briefs.bodyText:
State-owned NMDC has commissioned a 2 million tonne per annum (MTPA) pellet plant in Nagarnar, Chhattisgarh, as part of a ₹5,427-crore integrated iron ore processing, pipeline and pellet making project connecting its iron ore operations in Bacheli with the company’s steel plant in Nagarnar.
The project includes a new iron ore processing plant in Bacheli, a 15 MTPA slurry pipeline besides the 2 MTPA pellet plant. The 135 km slurry pipeline carries processed iron ore concentrate from Bacheli to Nagarnar, providing an alternative to transporting the material by road, the company said on Sunday.
The slurry pipeline passes through 61 villages in Bastar and Dantewada districts and is designed to reduce the movement of processed ore by road, provide alternate mode of evacuation and lower dependency on railways and ensures a dedicated link between Bacheli operations and Nagarnar, NMDC said.
The facilities will enable NMDC to process iron ore fines and slimes from its Bailadila mines into concentrate and subsequently convert them into pellets. The pellet plant uses Straight Grate Induration technology to produce pellets for use in steelmaking. The first production from the pellet plant was monitored live from NMDC’s headquarters by Chairman and Managing Director Amitava Mukherjee and the company’s senior leadership.
“This has not been an easy project to execute. It involved the processing facilities, the actual slurry pipeline and the pellet plant. Today is a red-letter day... when our collective dream is coming true,” Mr.Mukherjee said in a release.
NMDC said the commissioning strengthens its presence across the iron ore value chain, from mining and beneficiation to slurry transportation and pellet production. It also adds a new value-added product to the company’s portfolio and allows it to make greater use of iron ore fines and slimes generated from its Bailadila operations.
The project is part of the company’s broader expansion and diversification strategy, particularly as it eyes raising iron ore production capacity to 100 million tonnes in the long term.
Eyeing 60 MT iron ore output in FY27
Addressing the 68th annual general meeting of the company on Monday, the CMD said NMDC was targeting 60 million tonnes iron ore production in FY27 as “an important step towards the 100 MTPA pathway.
The plans follow the FY26 performance when NMDC became the first mining company in India to produce more than 50 MT of iron ore in a year. Production rose 20.62% to 53.16 MT and sales increased 13.15% to 50.24 MT, achieved organically by optimising existing equipment and infrastructure.
In a release, NMDC said it is embarking on a broad expansion programme, which ranges from slurry pipelines to AI-enabled mines and critical minerals exploration, to reshape its mining and logistics operations for the next phase of growth. The focus is on consolidating on the record production base, strengthening evacuation infrastructure, expanding mining capacity, deploying technology and diversifying into critical and strategic minerals.
Plans for ₹70,000 cr. investment
The company has outlined an investment roadmap of around ₹70,000 crore over five years for capacity expansion and modernisation, covering mining projects, beneficiation, evacuation infrastructure and technology.
“We are building an enterprise that is larger in scale, stronger in capability, smarter through technology and more responsible in its operations,” Mr. Mukherjee said.
The integrated slurry pipeline system, commissioned on September 26, comprises the iron ore processing plant in Bacheli, a 135-km slurry pipeline traversing three districts and the Nagarnar plant. It is expected to enhance evacuation capacity and improve the efficiency of the Bailadila value chain.
The Kirandul-Jagdalpur rail-line doubling has reached 98% progress, with 140 km completed and operational, adding freight evacuation capacity from the Bailadila sector.
The next phase of mining expansion depends on regulatory clearances. Management said it was pursuing environmental clearances for key operations, including the Kirandul and Bacheli complexes, to raise production in the near term and build towards 100 MTPA.
NMDC is also adding mineral assets. Tokisud North in Jharkhand began mining in January 2026, marking its entry into domestic coal mining. The company is also deploying a Digital Project Management Unit, automated sampling, digitally enabled drilling and blasting, real-time material visibility and integrated sustainability data systems, alongside automation, AI and predictive maintenance.

briefs.headline: ZEISS Group sees India’s tough operating terrain as global test lab
briefs.deck: For ZEISS, India’s toughest conditions may become the proving ground for some of the world’s most resilient precision technologies; Chennai facility would go beyond being an R&D centre to become part of its global innovation network
briefs.bodyText:
India’s extreme operating conditions — from high humidity and intense heat to dust, vibration and power fluctuations — are emerging as a real-world testing ground for technologies meant for some of the world’s most demanding industries, according to Andreas Pecher, President and CEO of ZEISS Group.
“Systems, devices and technologies capable of withstanding rigorous conditions in India will be robust enough to be exported globally for high-stakes sectors such as aerospace, maritime defence and heavy manufacturing,” Pecher told The Hindu in an exclusive interview.
The German technology major, which designs and manufactures high-precision medical devices, optoelectronic systems and advanced optical solutions, is looking at India not only as a growth market but also as a source of globally scalable innovation.
A key focus area under the initiative is harsh-environment optics— optical systems designed to deliver precision performance despite exposure to heat, dust, vibration and corrosive environments. Such technologies are increasingly critical in industrial quality assurance, manufacturing inspection and field applications.
India’s challenging environment provides a unique opportunity to develop solutions that are locally relevant but globally applicable, Mr. Pecher said. Technologies emerging from areas such as frugal engineering, robotics and advanced optics could eventually be integrated into ZEISS’s global operations across more than 50 countries.
The company believes India’s cost-conscious innovation ecosystem can help redesign product architectures without compromising precision or reliability.
Stressing that frugal innovation does not mean lower performance; he said it means rethinking designs and cost structures to create resource-efficient solutions using advanced technology.
The approach could allow ZEISS to reach new customer segments in emerging markets while improving competitiveness in developed economies.
ZEISS, which reported revenue of around €12 billion in September 2025, operates across semiconductor technology, industrial quality and research, manufacturing technology and consumer markets. The company invests nearly 15% of its annual revenue in research and development.
Mr. Pecher highlighted India’s engineering talent as a key advantage, noting that the country’s workforce has demonstrated the ability to solve complex problems under resource and cost constraints while maintaining high performance standards.
Chennai hub to connect deep-tech research with global markets
ZEISS’s recently launched innovation hub at the IIT Madras Research Park is expected to become a critical link between laboratory research and commercial applications.
Mr. Pecher said the Chennai facility would go beyond being an R&D centre and become part of ZEISS’s global innovation network, with intellectual property and technologies developed in India feeding into the company’s international product pipeline.
Research emerging from the collaboration will be evaluated for technical feasibility and commercial deployment, leveraging IIT Madras Research Park’s ecosystem of startups, laboratories and Centres of Excellence.
The Chennai initiative will follow a co-innovation model, bringing together ZEISS experts, IIT Madras faculty, researchers and startups to work on areas including robotics, fluid dynamics and optics.
Unlike a conventional venture capital or acquisition-led strategy, the partnership aims to jointly develop technologies by combining academic research, industry expertise and market access.
He said Chennai’s combination of industrial capability, engineering talent and challenging environmental conditions makes it particularly relevant for developing harsh-environment technologies.
“Successful technologies developed through this collaboration could move beyond the Indian market and enter ZEISS’s global product development pipeline,” he said.

stories.headline: From days without food to CWG gold: Ashmita faces India's 32-year judo wait at Asiad
stories.deck: Ashmita Dey carries a remarkable journey into the 2026 Asian Games after becoming the first Indian judoka to win Commonwealth Games gold. From growing up amid food shortages and a pawned gold earring to losing her father before the CWG, Dey has fought through financial hardship, injury and grief. Now a DSP in the Uttar Pradesh Police, she faces a strong Asian field and India's 32-year wait for…
stories.bodyText:
Ashmita Dey arrives at the Asian Games less than two months after becoming the first Indian judoka to win Commonwealth Games gold.
The Commonwealth title in Birmingham changed her profile almost overnight, and the 24-year-old, who had spent much of her career out of the spotlight, began to be recognised off the mat too.
“No one knew me before. But now everyone knows me. When I went to get food, someone said, this is the same girl, right? This is the same girl who created history for Judo for the first time in India. I was very happy to hear all this,” Ashmita told Timesofindia.com
The recognition means so much to her for a reason. Asmita’s career has been built through a combination of sporting support and financial uncertainty, with the latter shaping much of what she wanted from judo.
Before the Commonwealth gold, there had been the bronze at the Asian Junior Championships in 2022, gold at the Junior Asia Cup in Macau in 2023, a silver at the Asian Open in Kuwait later that year, and another podium finish at the African Open in Casablanca in 2025. She had also finished fifth at the Asian Senior Championships in Almaty in April this year.
The success and recognition have come a long way from a humble start in Belonia, a small town in Tripura, where her introduction to judo was almost accidental.
Her uncle heard about trials at a sports school where there was running, jumping and a fitness test. Asmita had initially been around athletics trials, but judo became the sport that stayed.
“My aunt thought I was talented and she put me in Judo and I started from there,” Asmita remembered.
Within a week of starting judo, she competed in a jiu-jitsu event and finished first. Two or three weeks later came a state competition, where she won gold.
The early years were sustained by family members moving her between places for training. Her brothers ferried her on a cycle for training, while her father would often travel with her from the village on a scooter, sometimes even in the rain.
“My father used to support me a lot. He never stopped me for a game. My mother never stopped me.”
When food was a struggle, a house became the dream
However, there were limits to what the family could provide. Asmita remembers periods when there was no food at home.
“Because sometimes we didn't even have food. We used to sleep after drinking water. Sometimes we only had rice, salt, and chillies with water. Sometimes we used to get food once, sometimes twice. So I remember all those days.”
Her mother had one gold earring, the only piece of jewellery she owned, and that was pawned for money. Asmita said she still has not been able to get it back, and the interest has continued to accumulate.
Asked if she would get it back now, Asmita’s answer was immediate.
“Yes, it will definitely come back. I have to get it.”
Her father worked as a bicycle mechanic, taking whatever work he could find as the family struggled to make ends meet. The family lived in rented accommodation for years. Asmita grew up with the idea that a house of their own would have to come from what she could achieve.
She had won her first competitions soon after starting, and her coaches were already telling her she could go further.
By 2018, she had won silver at the Khelo India Games and moved to the Sports Authority of India Regional Centre in Bhopal. That was when she came under coach Yashpal Solanki - former Indian judoka and an Arjuna Awardee - after earlier support from Manik Lal Deb in Tripura.
Asmit Dey with coach Yashpal Solanki
Solanki also pushed her towards international competition. “My coach used to say that I have to play internationally. I have to win a gold medal. He told me that I have to win a gold medal and have done that”
Father's death, Commonwealth gold and what followed
The path, most recently, was interrupted by injury and, more painfully, by the death of her father. When she was injured in Delhi, he had travelled to her with her medicines.
Asmita Dey with her Father
“When I was injured for the first time in Delhi, my father came to me. He brought all the medicines for me,” remembered Asmita.
His death, in 2025, came with a Commonwealth Games trial coming up, and her coach called her back to training around the 12th or 13th day.
There was about a month left.
“I told him that I can't do it. I don't want to do it.”
The coach then spoke to her about the Bhagavad Gita and death.
“He told me that this is the truth. He used to read the Gita. I also read the Gita. He told me that this is the truth. One day, a person has to go. He motivated me a lot.”
She returned to training. “To manage myself, I thought that if I cry and get weak, who will take care of my family? How will I make my house? I controlled my emotions a lot. You have to control your emotions a lot.”
And before the final, there was only one thought. “I was thinking that I have to win and I have to get the gold medal.”
She did, and the gold brought another reminder of the person she had lost. “Yes, I remembered my father a lot. If my father was alive, he would have been very happy. It was such a big achievement for me. He would have been very happy. I know that.”
But there was another moment on the Commonwealth podium that stayed with her: the Indian flag and the national anthem, with athletes from other countries standing around her.
“That was the biggest thing. I felt very proud.”
Ashmita joined the Uttar Pradesh Police in 2023 through the sports quota. She was subsequently promoted to sub-inspector and, after her Commonwealth Games gold, was elevated to deputy superintendent of police (DSP). The job had already given her a measure of financial security and helped her take care of herself and her family.
Asmita Dey has been promoted to DSP in UP Police
“I was so worried that I did so much in between. I have faced so much financially, but now I don't have to think much about that; I can [train with a] free mind. Now I can do better. I will do better.”
The house, though, remains on her mind.
“I always wanted to build a house. I had to do something. I had to do something big. Only if I do this, I can build a house. I always used to think like this. Finally, I can build a house now.”
A tough Asian Games test
Now comes the Asian Games, where Asmita will face a field led by several of Asia's established names in the women's -48kg category.
Mongolia's Narantsetseg Ganbaatar is the highest-ranked entrant at No. 13 in the world, followed by Kazakhstan's Abiba Abuzhakynova at No. 19. Japan's Mitsuki Kondo, Uzbekistan's Laziza Haydarova, Hong Kong China's Ka Lee Wong and South Korea's Su Jin Jung are also in the 11-judoka field.
There is another number that puts India's task in perspective. Judo has produced only five Asian Games medals for India, all of them bronze. Four came at the sport's debut at the 1986 Seoul Games, while Poonam Chopra won the fifth in the women's 56kg category at Hiroshima in 1994.
India has not been on the Asian Games judo podium since. Indian judokas, by comparison, have won 15 Commonwealth Games medals.
Asmita is entering a field led by higher-ranked Asian judokas, while carrying an Indian judo record that has not produced an Asian Games medal for 32 years.

stories.headline: Asian Games: India women’s compound archery team clinches gold, registers world record
stories.bodyText:
India win gold in the women’s compound team final after a perfect 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 in the final end. China shoots 10, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10 as India seals victory. India finishes on 238 points, matching South Korea’s world record. The final score is India 238-234.

Taniparthi Chikitha, Pradeep Prithika and Vennam Jyothi Surekha deliver a superb performance to beat China and finish with 238 points, with the defending Asian Games champions matching South Korea’s world record.
After the opening nine holes, Saptak Talwar is joint second at three-under par with a score of 32, helped by birdies on the second, third and fifth holes. Veer Ahlawat shoots 37, two-over par, after a double bogey on the first and an eagle on the eighth, along with bogeys on the fourth and ninth.
Yuvraj Sandhu cardes 34 after three birdies and two bogeys. The golf competition runs for four days, with medals decided at the end.
A nine would have taken the bronze medal match to a tie-break, while a 10 would have secured the medal for Chinese Taipei. But Chinese Taipei manage only an eight with its final shot, allowing South Korea to win the bronze medal.

briefs.headline: Gold against China! India’s women’s compound archers deliver Asian Games triumph
India's League of Legends team returns to Asiad with Hangzhou lessons
briefs.deck: Akshaj Shenoy returns to the Asian Games as captain of India's League of Legends team, three years after the side finished fifth in Hangzhou. Four players from that campaign return, joined by two Asian Games debutants. The group has since won in South Asia, competed against stronger regional opposition and joined S8UL. Now, against South Korea, Chinese Taipei and Hong Kong, they want to compete…
briefs.bodyText:
At 24, Akshaj Shenoy is heading back to the Asian Games as captain of India's League of Legends team. But becoming a professional player was never part of the original plan.
He started playing for fun. Then came the tournaments, better opponents and more time spent understanding the competitive side of the game. There was no single moment when he decided esports would become a profession.
“It happened gradually as I got better opportunities and started seeing how far I could take it,” Shenoy told Timesofindia.com.
By the time India reached the Asian Games in Hangzhou, Shenoy was studying Economics, Sociology and Industrial Relations while playing professionally and coordinating practice with teammates based in different cities.
Three years on, he is returning as the captain and four of the six players who will represent India in League of Legends at Aichi-Nagoya were part of the Hangzhou campaign, where India finished fifth. Ahmed Shahid and Rahul Bisht are the two newcomers.
“We look back at Hangzhou with a lot of pride, but also knowing that we could have gone further,” Shenoy said. “Once you've experienced that stage and seen that you can compete with some of the best teams in Asia, you naturally feel that there's more you can achieve.”
A game that demands five players to think as one
League of Legends is a 5v5 team-based strategy game in which players control unique characters, known as champions, and work together to destroy the opposing team’s Nexus, the central structure in their base. Each team has five roles, namely Top, Jungle, Mid, ADC and Support, with each serving a different function. Players have different roles and responsibilities, but at the professional level, communication and decision-making are as important as individual skill.
“You're constantly thinking about where the opponents could be, what they might do next and how you should respond,” Shenoy said. “At the same time, you're managing your own resources, positioning, timing and trying to make decisions based on what your teammates are doing.”
The game was launched in 2009 and has grown into one of the world's major esports titles, with professional competitions across regions and an annual World Championship.
For India, however, the challenge is less about finding people who play the game and more about creating enough high-level competition for players to develop against. Shenoy has seen that difference first-hand.
The group that stayed together
After Hangzhou, some of the Indian players continued competing together in domestic and South Asian League of Legends tournaments. They played more tournaments, won titles and spent more time as a unit. That continuity also gave them a better understanding of how each player communicates and reacts in different situations.
S8UL signed the group in 2025, giving the players a more structured environment around training and competition.
For S8UL co-founder and CEO Animesh Agarwal, that continuity is one of the roster's biggest strengths. He said the players had spent years “playing together, adapting to different competitive environments and developing a strong understanding of each other's game”.
The roster won Legends Ascend South Asia in 2025 and later competed in the LCP Promotion Wild Card Playoffs, finishing fifth.
“Playing against stronger regional teams gave us valuable experience and showed us where we still needed to improve,” Shenoy said.
Six players, six different routes
Shenoy is the most obvious link between the two Asian Games campaigns.
The Kochi-based 24-year-old was part of India's Hangzhou team and his esports career has run alongside education and work. Before Hangzhou, he was studying three subjects while playing professionally and coordinating practice sessions for teammates based in different cities. His parents, he said, were supportive of his choices.
Today, he is preparing for an MBA and helps with his father's business.
Back home, much of his day goes into studying and working on the business. Around 8 pm, he gets online with his teammates, with practice often continuing until 1 am because everyone has different studies and jobs to work around.
“I've always enjoyed gaming and, more importantly, the competitive side of esports, so it remains a big part of my life,” he said.
Mihir Ranjan is an IIM Ahmedabad graduate based in Delhi. Aakash Shandilya is from Noida and works as a cloud engineering intern. Sanindhya Malik is based in Mauritius and works with Telecommunications Consultants India Ltd.
Ahmed Shahid, a Chemical Engineering graduate from Aligarh, and 29-year-old Rahul Bisht, a product designer and entrepreneur from Bengaluru, are making their Asian Games debuts.
The six players arrive at Aichi-Nagoya with very different lives outside the game. For most of them, esports has had to fit around education, jobs and other responsibilities rather than replace them.
What Hangzhou left behind
The first Asian Games appearance gave Shenoy a different understanding of what it meant to play for India. “What I remember most is walking out there and realising that we were representing India on such a huge stage,” Shenoy said. “There was a lot of pride, but also a sense of responsibility that came with wearing the India jersey.”
The experience also showed the players what was required to compete against Asia's strongest teams. “We've had a few years since then to grow together, compete at a higher level and understand what it takes to perform on a stage like this,” he said.
The four returning players know what the stage feels like. Ahmed has been around the group for a long time despite making his Asian Games debut, while Rahul has adapted quickly during the preparations, according to Shenoy.
“At the end of the day, we trust each other, and my job is to make sure everyone feels comfortable enough to play their own game when the pressure is at its highest.”
The gap India is still trying to close
Shenoy has also seen India's esports environment become more organised since Hangzhou, with more tournaments, organisations and opportunities for players. But he believes the gap with the leading League of Legends regions remains clear.
“The biggest difference is probably the amount of regular high-level competition and the depth of the player pool,” Shenoy said.
In Korea, China and Vietnam, players are surrounded by strong competition and have more opportunities to test themselves against high-level opposition.
Indian players have had to be more proactive in finding those opportunities. “In India, we've had to be more proactive about finding those opportunities and learning from every international event we get to play,” Shenoy said.
Playing together consistently has helped the group develop its communication and understanding, while S8UL has provided a more professional environment around the team.
Joining the organisation, Shenoy said, gave the players more support with training and preparation and the confidence to look beyond India. “It also gave us more confidence to look beyond the Indian ecosystem and take international competition seriously,” he said.
But he sees a longer-term requirement for the game in India.
“There are more organisations, tournaments and opportunities for players to build a career,” Shenoy said. “At the same time, League of Legends still needs a deeper player pool and more regular high-level competition in India.”
For the next generation, he wants clearer pathways into competitive play. “The interest and talent are definitely there. The next step is building an ecosystem that can sustain that talent over the long term.”
South Korea, Chinese Taipei and Hong Kong await
India has been drawn alongside South Korea (2022 Asian Games Gold Medallist), Chinese Taipei (2022 Asian Games Silver Medallist) and Hong Kong in Group B at Aichi-Nagoya. For Shenoy, the group offers a direct measure of how much Indian League of Legends has developed.
The established Asian regions have deeper player pools and more regular high-level competition. Playing against them means testing how quickly the Indian players can make decisions, adapt and respond under pressure, but India is not travelling simply to observe.
“We don't want to go in thinking we're simply there to learn,” Shenoy said. “We've prepared seriously and we want to compete.”
“What they see on stage is the result of years of work behind the scenes,” he said. “There are countless hours of practice, travelling, studying the game and balancing esports with education, jobs and life outside gaming.”
“For us, wearing the India jersey is something we've worked towards for a long time. It's a huge responsibility, but it's also a privilege.”

briefs.headline: Sree Charani sets new ICC Women's T20I bowling record
briefs.deck: The left-arm spinner, who is already the top-ranked T20I bowler, reached a record rating of 817 points, surpassing the previous best mark of 806 points held by Australia’s Megan Schutt since November 2018.
briefs.bodyText:
India spinner Sree Charani has achieved the highest-ever rating points in the ICC Women’s T20I Bowling Rankings after her impressive performances in recent tournaments, according to the ICC website.
The left-arm spinner, who is already the top-ranked T20I bowler, reached a record rating of 817 points, surpassing the previous best mark of 806 points held by Australia’s Megan Schutt since November 2018.
Charani played a key role in India’s successful campaigns at the Women’s Asia Cup and then the Asian Games. She claimed 12 wickets during India’s Asia Cup-winning run, including a match-winning spell of 4/20 in the final against Sri Lanka as India lifted the title for the eighth time, according to the ICC website.
At the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, Charani continued her outstanding form, registering career-best figures of 4/10 against hosts Japan in the quarterfinals before taking two wickets in the gold medal match against Sri Lanka, helping India secure the title and boosting her rating to 817 points.
All-rounder Deepti Sharma also climbed in the T20I bowling rankings after taking three wickets in the Asian Games final, moving to a 754 rating. England’s Sophie Ecclestone remains third with 723 points. Meanwhile, India opener Smriti Mandhana returned to the top five of the ICC Women’s T20I Batting Rankings after scoring 79 runs in the Asian Games final against Sri Lanka.
In the ICC Women’s ODI Rankings, West Indies captain Hayley Matthews moved up three places to fourth among batters with 711 points following her record-breaking 182-run knock against Zimbabwe.Several Zimbabwe and West Indies players also made gains amid their ongoing ODI series. Zimbabwe’s Nyasha Gwanzura moved up 52 spots to 156th in the ODI bowling rankings after producing career-best figures of 4/33, while Modester Mupachikwa climbed 16 places to a career-best 40th in the batting rankings after scores of 86 and 38 in the series.
Australia’s Ash Gardner continues to lead the ODI all-rounder rankings, while Matthews remains at the top in the T20I all-rounder category. Alana King holds the No.1 spot in ODI bowling, Beth Mooney leads the T20I batting rankings, and Smriti Mandhana remains the top-ranked ODI batter.

briefs.headline: Akash Deep counts his blessings
briefs.deck: The pacer is returning to action for Rest of India against Jammu & Kashmir in the Irani Cup fixture from Thursday after spending seven months on the sidelines due to a stress fracture in his lower back. Having faced numerous hardships in his life, the 29-year-old, who notably finished with a match haul of 10 for 187 for India against England last year, speaks about how he dealt with the injury…
briefs.bodyText:
Akash Deep’s early years were engulfed by one ordeal after another. Sometime in 2010, he was in his teens when he had to leave his modest home in Bihar and move to neighbouring West Bengal on the pretext of finding a job. In 2015, he lost his father and elder brother in the space of a few months. Even in mid-2025, as he was bowling India to victory against England in the second Test at Edgbaston with a match haul of 10 for 187, his elder sister was battling cancer.
So when he found out in March this year that he would be sidelined for nearly seven months with a stress fracture in his lower back, he didn’t panic. Myriad curveballs had been thrown at the 29-year-old, and this was merely another that he had to deal with.
“I take everything positively. If I am injured today, I have the Centre of Excellence, a trainer, a physio and a coach. Even when I am practising, there are four or five members from the support staff. There are so many things set up for you to succeed. These are blessings,” Akash, donning a training jersey and shorts, said in a chat with The Hindu. “If I was still back in my village, there wouldn’t have been anyone to even tell me I am injured. I didn’t see this phase as needing mental toughness. There was nothing to be depressed about. I had such a well-drilled system looking after me. You have to just wake up and work hard. There is nothing else to think about. It is a blessing to have such things. So I was motivated and positive throughout.”
Akash was offering his perspective at a five-star hotel in Srinagar on Tuesday, two days out from the Irani Cup fixture between Rest of India and Jammu & Kashmir at the Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium. It will be his return to competitive action — his last outing was for Bengal against J&K in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy semifinal in February.
Vis-a-vis the hardships that life can entail beyond the sporting arena, a stress fracture may not be a tragedy. But it is no trivial matter either, for back injuries have derailed the careers of many promising fast bowlers.
The injury came about at the back end of a hectic season that saw Akash push the envelope in the quest to deliver Ranji glory for Bengal.
“When you are playing so much cricket through the year, I thought it was normal to feel stiffness. In the first innings of the semifinal, it was fine. In the second innings, I started feeling pain in my left glute and hamstring,” recalled Akash. “I didn’t feel anything in my back. We had a small total to defend. I took two wickets in six overs in the final session of day three. I was feeling stiffness overnight. But I thought I will get a break after the game for 7-8 days. I wanted to put in maximum effort. I bowled a spell of 10 overs with that on the morning of day four. While bowling, I didn’t feel much. But when my body cooled, I started feeling it. There was a camp in the CoE after that. They took a scan and it showed a stress fracture in the lower back.”
Till then, Akash hadn’t known what it would be like to miss so many months of cricket. But in keeping with his propensity to see the upside of every situation, he felt this was his body getting its wish for a breather.
“By God’s grace, the good thing in my case has been that I have recovered very quickly from injuries. I knew that even if it is a stress fracture, I would recover well if I followed all the processes correctly. Yes, I would have to miss some cricket. But I also felt that my body was demanding rest. I had been playing regularly for 8-9 years. I had never taken a very long break. Even when I had injuries, I had to miss cricket for a month at the most. I didn’t take it in a negative way,” he said.
Recovery and rehab
While the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence (CoE) has faced severe flak recently for the recurring injuries that many of India’s top players have encountered, Akash was generous in his praise of the state-of-the-art facility. So much so that he willingly returned to Bengaluru soon after his marriage in June.
“The people at CoE have a lot of experience. They have seen a lot of cases. Around 10 days after the injury was diagnosed, they put the entire plan and timeline in place. It has all gone accordingly. Neither I nor they missed a beat. In the initial stages, which was about rest and strengthening the core, I was going back home occasionally. But after my marriage, I was at CoE all through. If there is time on your hands, there is no better facility than CoE for practice, gym and recovery,” he asserted.
The months at CoE, according to Akash, were put to very good use.
“I analysed a lot about how I can spend this time productively. I started focusing on every aspect. I spoke to a dietitian about how I can improve my diet further. Things like muscle training, how much to sleep… I realised that I have to use this time well to prolong my career. I hope I don’t have to spend so much time on the sidelines again. I went into every little detail as an athlete,” informed the seamer from the town of Sasaram.
Understanding his body
Keeping Akash company at different junctures were the likes of Jasprit Bumrah, Hardik Pandya and Mayank Yadav. All of them have had a history of acute back injuries.
“I asked them about the things I wanted to know, but the main thing is how does your body respond. That is the main lesson I’ve learnt from these months. I learnt about how my body reacts to different things like diet, training and sleep. It is very important to read your body as an athlete. That was a big takeaway,” opined Akash.
Another learning is knowing when to operate at full tilt and when to apply the brakes.
It is admittedly a hard balancing act whilst being in the heat of the battle. Having entered the domestic season on the back of a breakthrough performance at Edgbaston, Akash seems to think he exerted himself a tad too much.
“After that England series, which was a lot of fun to play, I exerted a lot of effort in domestic cricket. I should have understood my body more,” he felt.
“But when you are in the thick of the action, you tend to forget a lot of things. You just give it your all. You can never know about injuries. You have to play through phases. You don’t know what that can lead to. To be honest, if it is a do-or-die match, it is very hard to hold back. But I can try to be smarter about situations where it is needed and where it is not needed.”
An eye on Kiwiland
If Akash’s comeback goes smoothly in Srinagar, his focus will gradually turn towards making the cut for the Test tour of New Zealand.
Scheduled in November, in the early stages of the Black Caps’ home season, Akash’s knack for extracting seam movement should make him an enticing pick in the southern hemisphere. “My strength is bowling long spells and at a consistent spot. My focus will be on that,” he explained.
“You may have practised for 7-8 months, but a match is different. I have to get used to the rigour of playing matches. You may sustain yourself physically, but it is also about sustaining mentally for six hours for five days. That can only come from game time. So I have to get used to these things. Whenever I get a chance, I will keep myself ready to deliver.”
If there are any concerns about how soon Akash can find his rhythm, the seamless start he made to his Test career against England in Ranchi, with three wickets in his opening spell, is instructive. He may be still new to the Test fold, but knows his craft thoroughly by virtue of his extensive grind in the domestic circuit.
“I had played 40-45 First Class matches by the time I played Test cricket,” he said. “So, I had that advantage. I had that confidence. When you are performing consistently in domestic cricket, you know how to perform regardless of the situation and batter. “I knew my strengths. I knew I just had to keep doing the same things that I had been doing for around four years.”

briefs.headline: With eye on New Zealand tour, BCCI to issue Ranji Trophy diktat
briefs.deck: With India's tour of New Zealand set to begin on October 22, the mental preparations have already begun. Ahead of the bumper five T20I, five ODI and two Test series, the key members of the Test squad would be required to play domestic cricket to stay fit and match sharp.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India are set to lock horns with New Zealand in a crucial away two-Test series starting November 15 and the think-tank has already commenced planning for the assignment. TimesofIndia.com has learnt that the team management, including all members of the selection committee, was in a huddle before the 2nd ODI against the West Indies in Guwahati.
It has been unanimously agreed that the Test hopefuls will be asked to play for their respective states in the Ranji Trophy, which begins on October 11. Both captain Shubman Gill and vice-captain 
KL Rahul
 are set to lead the preparation talk as they are likely to play for Punjab and Karnataka, respectively, in at least one group stage fixture.
"The match and the number of matches they play will depend on the medical team's clearance, keeping the workload and assignments in mind. We must factor in that some players participate in two formats. Accordingly, a decision will be made, but participation will not be compromised. All senior players, including the captain, are expected to play at least one game provided there are no medical/workload concerns," says an official tracking developments.
Conversations have already begun regarding Jasprit Bumrah's planning for the tour. The team management wants him to have some red-ball volume before playing the series opener in mid-November. The options on the table are either one Ranji Trophy fixture for Gujarat or the India A game when the squad assembles for the three fixtures starting October 24.
The T20I team will be in action at the same time so there well could be a window for Bumrah to squeeze in a First Class fixture but it could be close for comfort as the ODI series starts November 4 in Auckland. So it remains to be seen how the management charts his route, but volume will remain the keyword.
The fast bowling core identified for the New Zealand Tests comprising Mohammed Siraj, Gurnoor Brar, Prasidh Krishna, Auqib Nabi and Akash Deep will also be asked to get enough overs under their belt.
Special focus will be on Akash as the team management is very excited to have him back in the set up and will closely monitor his progress starting with the Irani Cup tie in Srinagar.
Another player who will be keenly tracked is all-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy, more for his bowling because he will lend the crucial balance to the Playing XI.
With Ajit Agarkar unlikely to get an extension as the chief selector, Pragyan Ojha could well chair the selection meeting when the men who matter assemble to pick squads for the tour of New Zealand. As TimesofIndia.com first reported, Parthiv Patel is frontrunner to replace Agarkar from West Zone and become the new chairman but the formalities could take some time.

briefs.headline: Al Fursan-led consortium acquires Kerala Blasters FC from Magnum Group
briefs.deck: The takeover ends the tenure of Hyderabad-based Magnum Sports, which had owned and managed the club since 2016
briefs.bodyText:
KOCHI: A consortium led by UAE-based Al Fursan Group has taken complete ownership of 
Kerala Blasters FC
, one of the most popular clubs in the 
Indian Super League
. The announcement was made at a news conference in Kochi on Tuesday. Club officials did not disclose the value of the transaction, but sources indicate that the deal is worth about Rs 120 crore, placing it among the largest foreign investments in Indian football in recent years.
The takeover ends the tenure of Hyderabad-based Magnum Sports, which had owned and managed the club since 2016. Kerala Blasters CEO Abhik Chatterjee said the ownership transfer will be carried out in phases and is expected to be completed over the next eight months.
Under the new arrangement, the club’s operations will be managed by Ofioh Sporty. Its CEO, Thameem Anvar, said the new owners have plans to develop a dedicated stadium for the Blasters. He added that more details would be revealed once “Project Blasters” is formally announced.
There had been speculation that the club could shift its base to Kozhikode, but Chatterjee clarified that Kochi will remain Kerala Blasters’ home. 
The team will continue to play its home matches at the Jawaharlal Nehru International Stadium. Addressing expectations for the upcoming season, he said the club’s ambition to win remains strong, though preparations are limited by time. He also confirmed that Ashley Westwood will continue as head coach and will take decisions on squad matters.
Chatterjee dismissed reports suggesting that the Blasters’ opening home match could be postponed. He said delaying the fixture would be unfair to other teams because the league schedule has already been released.
Al Fursan Group is understood to have backing from business interests connected to Sharjah’s ruling Al Qasimi family. Its entry gives a Gulf-based investment group control of a club with one of the largest fan bases in Indian football.
The acquisition comes as Kerala Blasters prepare for the 2026-27 ISL season. Magnum Sports had been seeking a buyer, and interested parties completed financial, legal and operational due diligence before the sale was finalised.
